title: A LIGHTWEIGHT HYBRID QUANTUM CLASSICAL FEDERATED LEARNING MODEL FOR ANOMALY DETECTION IN EDGE IOT NETWORKS
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The number of IoT devices continues to rise and it is imperative to detect anomalies in real-time to ensure the security, reliability and efficiency of the system. Current deep neural network models have great memory and computing requirements, so it is not easy to use on the edge device. The benefit of federated learning is that it leaves raw data on the individual device, thus improving privacy. Nonetheless, efficient feature learning by compressing the size of quantum datasets has not been built into current federated learning frameworks, and the efficacy of quantum-based approaches under realistic noise in the hardware have not been widely investigated. To address privacy concerns, QEdgeNet is a lightweight hybrid quantum-classical federated learning (QLFL) model for anomaly detection in edge-IoT networks . In this model, the features of network traffic are first compressed by principal component analysis, and then the network traffic is mapped to a compact 4-qubit variational quantum circuit for the classification of anomalous traffic. This model is an aggregated model updated using the Cheon-Kim-Kim-Song (CKKS) homomorphic encryption mechanism, but without exposing the raw network data of clients, and raw traffic data never escapes from a client device during the training process. The applicability of the suggested approach in an idealized simulator is quantified by measuring the inference performance in a simulator simulated quantum hardware noise, the accuracy loss from the hardware noise is recovered by extrapolating to zero noise.

abstract: This software and experiment package provides the reproducibility materials for a comparative study of Variational Quantum Classification (VQC) and Quantum Kernel Alignment (QKA) for binary network intrusion detection using the UNSW-NB15 benchmark dataset. title: Hardware-Aware Tensor Networks for Real-Time Quantum-Inspired Anomaly Detection at Particle Colliders
abstract: Quantum machine learning offers the ability to capture complex correlations in high-dimensional feature spaces, crucial for the challenge of detecting beyond the Standard Model physics in collider events, along with the potential for unprecedented computational efficiency in future quantum processors. The cascaded SMPO architecture is introduced as an SMPO variation that affords greater flexibility and efficiency in ways that are key to edge applications in resource-constrained environments. These results reveal the benefit and near-term feasibility of deploying quantum-inspired ML in high energy colliders.

title: Quantum-Inspired Intrusion Detection System Using Dual Metaheuristic Optimization and Deep Neural Analysis
venue: International Conference on Intelligent Data Communication Technologies and Internet of Things (IDCIoT)
abstract: The high rate of cyber threat development poses serious threats to the traditional Intrusion Detection System (IDS) that in most cases fail to detect effectively and falsely alarms when handling high volumes of high dimensional network traffic. In order to overcome these weaknesses, this study suggests a Quantum-inspired Hybrid IDS and it combines dual metaheuristic optimization and quantum-classical Deep Learning (DL) models. The framework initially preprocesses the raw network traffic data and then, the proposed Self-Adaptive Grasshopper-Whale Optimization Algorithm (SAGWOA) is employed to select features efficiently, i.e., to reduce the number of data dimensions and maintain important data. To enhance the nonlinear learning ability, Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) is utilized which exploits quantum superposition and entanglement concepts. Besides, the proposed Quantum aided Deep Convolutional Support Vector Machine (QDC-SVM) is used for learning spatial and hierarchical patterns and performing quantum-enhanced classification. Here, the Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) is used to enable the deep feature learning and Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM) is employed to increase the margin separation between normal and attack traffic. Experimental analysis on benchmark datasets, such as NSL-KDD and CICIDS2017 shows the proposed hybrid IDS performs superior, in terms of detection accuracy (98.64 and 98.66% respectively) and lower false alarm rates (0.049% and 0.016% respectively), in comparison with traditional solutions.

title: Space Mission Quantum GenAI and XAI System for Predictive Anomaly Detection and Mission Optimization
abstract: Humanity’s exploration of space has reached unprecedented levels of complexity. This work establishes a foundation for fully autonomous, quantum-enhanced space mission planning, capable of both prediction and explanation in highly uncertain environments.

title: Evaluation of Variational Quantum Classifiers (VQC) for Cyberattack Detection in the NISQ Era
venue: Journal of Sensor and Actuator Networks
abstract: We investigate the structural limits of Variational Quantum Classifiers (VQC) for network anomaly detection in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era. Using the official 20% research subset of NSL-KDD, we train a 4-qubit classifier that embeds 16 principal components by amplitude encoding and reaches 88% accuracy on the held-out partition. On the four established attack families, an explicit many-to-one decoding of the sixteen basis outcomes attains 71.8% in-sample accuracy and a macro-averaged recall of 0.787 on held-out attack records, against 0.250 for a majority-class classifier. Aggregate accuracy conceals that separation entirely: 78.4% for the trained model against 78.7% for the trivial one. Measuring class separability in the encoded states before training, amplitude encoding retains an AUC of 0.560±0.018 at sixteen components over five seeds, against 0.762±0.020 for angle encoding. Yet a trained comparison at matched parameter count on four components converts none of that advantage into accuracy: the separation is present in the encoded geometry and absent from the classifier, which implicates the readout alongside the encoding, a distinction this design does not separate. A controlled sweep over five ansatz depths and five seeds, spanning 8 to 72 trainable parameters at fixed encoding, data and decoding, finds subsample accuracy saturating at 0.880±0.005 while the training objective keeps falling, with a parameter-matched circuit trailing a 73-parameter classical network by 7.9 points across the two protocols compared. Depth is therefore not the binding constraint. On KDDTest+, classical recall on novel signatures falls by 19 to 32 points while the variational classifier shows no comparable decline.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Security for Edge-IIoT: Robust Intrusion Detection with a Novel Quantum-Classical Neural Network
abstract: The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things in critical industrial environments has significantly increased the attack surface, exposing systems to sophisticated cyber threats. Traditional pattern-based intrusion detection systems struggle to detect such advanced attacks, while deep learning approaches, despite achieving high detection accuracy, often suffer from high computational cost and latency, limiting their deployment in resource-constrained edge gateways. Quantum machine learning offers a promising alternative by enabling high-dimensional feature representation; however, current implementations are constrained by hardware noise, limited qubit availability and backend-dependent execution characteristics in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum era. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a Residual Hybrid Quantum-Classical Neural Network (RHQ-CNN) for efficient intrusion detection in Edge-Industrial Internet of Things (Edge-IIoT) environments under idealized quantum simulation conditions. The proposed framework employs a classical neural network encoder to compress high-dimensional network traffic into a compact latent representation suitable for quantum processing. A variational quantum circuit with serial data re-uploading is then utilised to model complex non-linear decision boundaries without increasing qubit requirements. In addition, a residual connection fuses classical and quantum representations to improve training stability and preserve latent feature information. The model is evaluated on the Edge-IIoTset dataset and achieves a test accuracy of 99.94%, with high weighted performance across the 15-class detection task, although the extremely low-sample Fingerprinting class remains comparatively more challenging. Additional controlled ablation, deployment-cost, and bootstrap confidence interval analyses demonstrate the test-set metric stability and computational trade-offs of the proposed architecture. These findings highlight the potential of hybrid quantum-classical models for next-generation cybersecurity in industrial IoT systems.

title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical GANs for the Generation of Adversarial Network Flows
abstract: Classical generative adversarial networks (GANs) have been applied to generate adversarial network traffic capable of attacking intrusion detection systems, but they suffer from shortcomings such as the need for large amounts of high-dimensional datasets, mode collapse, and high computational overhead. In this work, we propose a hybrid quantum-classical GAN (QC-GAN) framework where a variational quantum generator is used to generate synthetic network traffic flows mimicking malicious traffic using latent representations. Instead of sampling classical noise vectors, we encode the latent vector (the hidden features) as a quantum state, which is the basis for claiming more expressive latent representations and reducing computational overhead. A classical discriminator will be trained on real-world datasets (UNSW-NB15) and the proposed QC-GAN-generated fake network flows. In this configuration, the generator aims to minimize the discriminator's ability to distinguish real from fake traffic, while the discriminator aims to maximize its classification accuracy, in an iterative manner. In our attack model, we assume that the attacker is a state actor with access to limited quantum computing power, whereas the discriminator is chosen to be classical, as will likely be the case for most end users and organizations. We test the generated flows using classical intrusion detection system (IDS) models, such as a random forest classifier and a convolutional neural network-based classifier, for their ability to bypass the detection process. This work aims to highlight the possibilities of quantum machine learning as a means of generating advanced attack flows and stress testing classical IDS. Lastly, we further evaluate how hardware-based noise affects these attacks to offer a new perspective on IDS, highlighting the need for a quantum resilient defense system.

title: Asymmetric class-conditional routing in a federated quantum mixture-of-experts improves imbalanced intrusion detection in edge industrial IoT networks
abstract: Intrusion detection systems (IDS) deployed in Edge Industrial Internet of Things (Edge-IIoT) environments face three critical and interrelated challenges: (i) extreme class imbalance, where tail-class attack categories may be outnumbered by benign traffic at ratios exceeding 700:1; (ii) competitive expert collapse in gating mechanisms relying on softmax normalization, which prevents sparse, class-conditional routing; and (iii) statistical heterogeneity across geographically distributed edge nodes with non-IID local traffic distributions. Existing federated learning solutions address these challenges in isolation, yielding suboptimal tail-class detection. We propose FedQMoE-IDS , a novel federated quantum mixture-of-experts framework that jointly resolves all three challenges through three synergistic innovations: (1) a class-balanced asymmetric focal loss with per-class focusing parameters \(\gamma _c\) that independently modulate head- and tail-class gradients via effective-number weighting; (2) a normalized sigmoid gating mechanism with auxiliary-loss-free dynamic bias load balancing, replacing softmax to achieve genuine sparse activation with exact zero weights and class-conditional expert routing; and (3) a selective federated aggregation strategy that partitions the parameter space into shared (FedDyn-aggregated CNN+KAN+classifier), locally retained (personalized gating networks), and periodically exchanged (variational quantum circuit experts) components. The three-stage MoE architecture cascades 1D-CNN feature extractors, variational quantum circuit (VQC) encoders operating in Hilbert space, and Kolmogorov–Arnold Network (KAN) spline experts, each governed by independent sigmoid top- K gates. We conduct experiments under a realistic non-IID federated setting with \(N{=}10\) Edge-IIoT clients partitioned via a Dirichlet distribution ( \(\alpha {=}0.3\) ), and we compare against parameter-matched classical baselines (deeper CNN and softmax-gated MoE), personalized federated MoE (FedMoE, pFedMoE), and federated class-imbalance methods. Comprehensive experiments on UNSW-NB15, Edge-IIoTset, and CIC-IDS2017 with five-seed evaluation and Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon signed-rank tests demonstrate that FedQMoE-IDS achieves 99.20% accuracy and 98.40% macro F1-score on UNSW-NB15, and 99.80% accuracy on Edge-IIoTset—surpassing recent state-of-the-art methods including centralized deep learning, federated LSTM, and transformer-based IDS. All improvements are statistically significant ( \(p < 0.05\) ). The full source code and configuration files are publicly available to enable independent reproduction.

title: Adaptive-Shot Hybrid Quantum Anomaly Detection for Tactile Internet Security: Reliability-Aware Measurement Allocation Under Resource Constraints
abstract: Tactile Internet (TI) security analytics must balance reliable thresholded decisions with constrained computational and measurement resources. We study this tension for finite-shot hybrid quantum anomaly inference and introduce the Adaptive-Shot Variational Quantum Circuit (AS-VQC) policy. This validation-calibrated policy begins each record at 128 shots and cumulatively escalates through 256, 512, and 1024 shots only when the finite-shot anomaly score remains close to a validation-selected security threshold. The quantum scorer is evaluated as an off-path security analytics component rather than part of the haptic critical path. Using a 4,875-record CESNET-TimeSeries24-derived aggregate-flow benchmark, leakage-safe random, entity-group-disjoint, and temporal holdouts, and five trained quantum neural network (QNN) checkpoints per holdout, the primary AS-VQC-95 (beta = 0.95) policy averages 129.2, 276.9, and 131.2 shots per record, saving 87.4%, 73.0%, and 87.2% of the uniform 1024-shot baseline (Fixed-1024), respectively. The decision disagreement with analytic (exact-expectation) inference is 0.771%, 0.409%, and 0.635%, lower than both the uniform 128-shot baseline (Fixed-128) and a matched-budget shuffled-allocation control. Fixed-1024 remains more decision-stable, establishing a measurable reliability-resource trade-off rather than cost-free equivalence. A more conservative AS-VQC-99 (beta = 0.99) further reduces disagreement while using fewer than 512 average shots across all holdouts. These results show that finite quantum measurements can be treated as an inference resource and concentrated on boundary-sensitive TI-security decisions while exposing checkpoint-dependent escalation under unseen-entity conditions.

title: Quantum-Resilient Federated Intrusion Detection: A Hybrid Quantum Classical Framework For Safeguarding U.S. Critical Infrastructure In The Post-Quantum Era

abstract: Large scale quantum computation poses a threat to the public-key based encryption that protects the privacy of communications traversing U.S. critical infrastructure and defense networks. title: Multi-Path Parallel Quantum Convolutional Neural Network
abstract: Quantum Convolutional Neural Networks (QCNN) migrate the convolution and pooling concepts of classical Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) to variational quantum circuits, showing potential on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices. However, traditional QCNN adopts a single-depth circuit structure, which has limitations in multi-scale feature extraction, and is prone to the barren plateau phenomenon during training, making it difficult to adapt to high-dimensional real-world scenarios such as network intrusion detection. This paper proposes a QCNN architecture based on a multi-path parallel structure. For the network intrusion detection task, it draws on the Inception module to construct three parallel quantum convolution paths: shallow, medium, and deep, achieving hierarchical extraction of multi-scale features; residual connections are introduced to preserve encoded state information and provide gradient shortcuts; a hybrid optimization strategy combining classical Adam and Quantum Natural Gradient (QNG) is adopted to adapt to the heterogeneous parameter space. Experimental validation shows that, on the UNSW-NB15 network intrusion detection dataset, the proposed Multi-Path Parallel Quantum Convolutional Neural Network (MP-QCNN) improves detection accuracy by 3% compared to traditional single-path QCNN and effectively mitigates the barren plateau phenomenon. This design strictly maintains NISQ depth constraints and quantum parallelism advantages, providing an efficient and stable feature extraction framework for high-dimensional tasks such as network intrusion detection.

title: Harnessing Quantum Kernels for Supervised Learning: A Deep Dive into Quantum SVMs

title: Integrating Quantum-Classical Attention in Patch Transformers for Enhanced Time Series Forecasting
abstract: QCAAPatchTF is a quantum attention network integrated with an advanced patch-based transformer, designed for multivariate time series forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection. It then applies the quantum-classical hybrid self-attention mechanism alongside a feed-forward network in the encoder stage of the advanced patch-based transformer. title: Optimal Quantum Variational Circuits for Detecting False Data Injection Attacks on Transmission Substations

The proposed QIDS leverages Quantum Variational Circuits (QVCs), a quantum machine learning circuit architecture with trainable parameters, that can be trained offline to distinguish manipulated relay measurements from those arising from faults. We test the performance of the optimized QIDS under a comprehensive set of FDIA and fault scenarios generated in an OPAL-RT HYPERSIM environment. Our results confirm that the proposed QIDS can accurately detect malicious FDIA values without compromising the relay's protective dependability. The performance of the proposed QIDS is also evaluated under measurement noise, measurement errors, sophisticated attacks, and varying measurement window sizes and sampling rates, and is further compared against existing methods. abstract: One-class classification (OCC) is a fundamental problem in machine learning with numerous applications, such as anomaly detection and quality control. title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Algorithms for Quantum Computing Applications in Computational Physics
abstract: Computational methods are central to modern physics, yet many problems, especially those involving Quantum Many-Body Systems (QMBSs), remain challenging at scale. The core difficulty of simulating QMBSs is the exponential growth of the solution space with system size. This renders exact treatments intractable and pushes approximate methods to their limits when tackling two- and higher-dimensional systems and long-time dynamics. Quantum computers offer a quantum-native platform for representing and manipulating such systems. Recent algorithmic and technological advancements have enabled experiments on quantum processors in the quantum utility regime, a scale at which exact classical reproduction is no longer feasible. This represents the first step towards realizing quantum advantage, where quantum computers solve specific, practically relevant problems more efficiently than any classical approach. While advancing towards the goal of quantum advantage, useful computations on quantum processors are expected to be realised through hybrid quantum-classical algorithms, which combine quantum experiments and classical computational resources. A prominent example are variational quantum algorithms, where a Parametrized Quantum Circuit (PQC) prepares a trial quantum state whose parameters are iteratively updated by a classical optimisation routine to minimize a target cost function (e.g., the energy of a target Hamiltonian). However, the optimisation of such PQCs is affected by trainability issues, such as barren plateaus in the parameter landscape, which can render the optimisation increasingly difficult for larger system sizes. This motivates the development of novel hybrid approaches overcoming the limits of PQCs. In this thesis, we introduce a new class of approaches based on hybrid Tensor Networks (TNs). A hybrid TN is obtained by integrating quantum states prepared on a quantum processor within TNs -- one of the state-of-the-art approaches for simulating quantum systems. We first show how hybrid TNs can be used for ground-state searches within a variational setting. Then, we further extend the framework to non-variational hybrid TN ansätze for which the quantum tensors are prepared via quantum annealing and subsequently post-processed by classical TNs. In the context of quantum machine learning, which also relies on PQCs, we further investigate heuristic best practices that mitigate the same exponential concentration effects in kernel-based models for anomaly detection. Another class of hybrid algorithms are quantum error-mitigation workflows, where classical post-processing is used to reconstruct expectation values from noise-affected circuit executions. Such methods generally feature a trade-off between the bias and the variance: the price to pay for mitigating noise in a bias-free fashion is that the number of measurements usually grows exponentially with the depth of the circuit in order to achieve a fixed accuracy. In this thesis, we develop a low-resource error-mitigation strategy that reduces the measurement overhead in practical digital Hamiltonian-simulation workflows. We apply this method to Trotterized dynamics in a lattice-gauge-theory model, enabling the extraction of expectation values with improved accuracy at time-scales that allow the observation of post-collision scattering dynamics.

abstract: The rapid growth of digital technologies has transformed data from a supporting resource into one of the most valuable assets for modern organizations, scientific research, engineering, healthcare, business, and society. Every digital interaction generates data, while advances in cloud computing, artificial intelligence, machine learning, distributed systems, and emerging computational technologies have created unprecedented opportunities to transform this data into meaningful knowledge and actionable intelligence. However, the ability to collect large volumes of data alone does not guarantee meaningful outcomes. Effective data intelligence requires a strong foundation in mathematical modelling, statistical reasoning, data engineering, machine learning, analytical discovery, responsible artificial intelligence, and intelligent decision-making. With this perspective, we have developed Data Intelligence: Mathematical Models, Machine Learning and Analytical Discovery as a comprehensive academic textbook for students, educators, researchers, and professionals seeking to understand the principles and applications of modern data intelligence. The book is designed to establish a progressive learning pathway, beginning with mathematical and statistical foundations, moving through data engineering and machine learning, advancing toward modern analytical intelligence and generative AI, and concluding with practical case studies, responsible AI, and future directions. The central objective of this book is to bridge the gap between theoretical foundations and practical analytical applications. Mathematics provides the language through which data relationships can be represented and analysed, statistics provides the principles for reasoning under uncertainty, data engineering provides the infrastructure for preparing and managing information, and machine learning provides computational methods for discovering patterns and making predictions. Modern developments such as generative AI, large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, multimodal intelligence, AI agents, federated learning, quantum machine learning, digital twins, and autonomous analytics further extend the possibilities of data-driven intelligence. The book therefore approaches data intelligence as an integrated discipline rather than as a collection of isolated technologies. Chapter 1, Foundations of Data Intelligence and Mathematical Models, establishes the conceptual and mathematical foundation of the subject. It begins with the evolution, concepts, and scope of data intelligence and examines how data ecosystems, data sources, data lifecycles, and data-driven decision-making contribute to intelligent organizations. The chapter introduces vectors, matrices, tensors, and linear algebra, followed by probability, statistics, and statistical inference. Correlation, covariance, regression, statistical models, optimization, gradient methods, and mathematical modelling are subsequently discussed. The chapter also emphasizes data quality, data governance, data management, privacy, ethics, and responsible data intelligence, providing an essential foundation for the chapters that follow. Chapter 2, Data Engineering, Analytics and Machine Learning, focuses on the transformation of raw data into analytical information and machine learning knowledge. Data collection, integration, cleaning, and transformation are presented as essential components of reliable analytical systems. Exploratory data analysis and analytical visualization are introduced to help learners understand patterns, distributions, relationships, and trends within datasets. The chapter then develops important machine learning concepts including feature engineering, dimensionality reduction, supervised learning, regression, classification, decision trees, ensemble learning, support vector machines, clustering, association rule mining, recommendation systems, and customer analytics. Particular attention is given to model training, validation, evaluation, and optimization so that learners understand not only how models are developed but also how their performance and reliability are assessed. Chapter 3, Advanced Machine Learning and Analytical Discovery, moves from foundational machine learning toward advanced computational intelligence. Neural networks and deep learning architectures are introduced as powerful approaches for learning complex representations from data. Convolutional, recurrent, and transformer-based models are explored in relation to visual data, sequential information, language, and other complex analytical tasks. Time-series forecasting and predictive intelligence demonstrate how historical observations can support future-oriented analysis. The chapter further addresses anomaly, fraud, and risk detection, followed by explainable and interpretable machine learning. Causal AI and causal discovery introduce methods for understanding cause-and-effect relationships rather than relying exclusively on statistical associations. Prescriptive analytics, decision intelligence, automated machine learning, and intelligent analytical discovery complete the chapter by demonstrating how analytical systems can progress from prediction toward recommendations and automated knowledge discovery. Chapter 4, Generative AI, Emerging Technologies and Applications, examines the rapidly evolving technologies that are redefining contemporary data intelligence. Generative AI, large language models, and foundation models are presented as important components of modern intelligent systems. Retrieval-augmented generation and knowledge-based intelligence demonstrate how external knowledge can be integrated with generative models. The chapter explores multimodal intelligence, AI agents, and agentic analytics, emphasizing systems capable of processing diverse information and supporting complex analytical workflows. Real-time and streaming data intelligence, cloud and edge computing, synthetic data, vector databases, and knowledge graphs are discussed as important components of modern data platforms. Federated learning, privacy-preserving AI, quantum machine learning, digital twins, autonomous analytics, and Industry 5.0 further demonstrate the interdisciplinary evolution of data intelligence. The chapter concludes by examining advanced applications across healthcare, finance, manufacturing, energy, and smart cities. Chapter 5, Case Studies, Responsible AI and Future Directions, connects the concepts developed throughout the book with realistic application scenarios. Healthcare applications demonstrate disease prediction and personalized healthcare, while finance applications examine credit risk and intelligent fraud detection. Retail analytics explores customer segmentation and recommendation intelligence. Manufacturing applications focus on predictive maintenance and industrial intelligence. Smart city and energy applications demonstrate traffic and energy demand forecasting, while cybersecurity applications address intelligent anomaly and intrusion detection. A dedicated generative AI case study examines enterprise knowledge discovery using large language models and retrieval-augmented generation. The final section considers the future of data intelligence through responsible AI, autonomous analytics, and AI-native data platforms. A distinguishing feature of this book is its emphasis on the relationship between mathematical foundations, computational methods, analytical reasoning, and real-world decision-making. Learners are encouraged to understand not only what an algorithm does, but also why it works, what assumptions it makes, how its performance should be evaluated, and where it can be applied responsibly. Mathematical and statistical concepts are therefore connected with machine learning and analytical applications throughout the book. This approach is intended to support both conceptual understanding and practical problem-solving. We have also given considerable importance to the principles of responsible data intelligence. The increasing deployment of AI systems creates important questions concerning privacy, security, fairness, transparency, accountability, interpretability, governance, and human oversight. Data-driven systems can influence healthcare decisions, financial services, industrial operations, public infrastructure, and individual experiences. Consequently, technical capability must be accompanied by responsible design and appropriate governance. The book treats responsible AI not as an independent topic but as a continuing consideration across the data intelligence lifecycle. The book is intended to serve a broad academic audience. abstract: The rapid convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) has given rise to a transformative technological paradigm known as the Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT). From smart cities and intelligent healthcare to Industry 5.0, autonomous transportation, precision agriculture, and sustainable energy systems, AIoT has become the cornerstone of next-generation digital transformation. The book "Engineering Intelligent AIoT Systems: Artificial Intelligence for Smart Connected Technologies" has been developed to provide students, researchers, academicians, engineers, and industry professionals with a comprehensive understanding of intelligent AIoT technologies and their engineering applications. This book presents a balanced integration of theoretical foundations, practical implementation strategies, emerging technologies, industrial case studies, and future research directions that reflect the rapidly evolving AIoT landscape. The content is carefully organized into five comprehensive chapters, each addressing a major dimension of intelligent AIoT engineering. Chapter 1 introduces the foundational concepts of AIoT, beginning with the evolution from traditional IoT to intelligent AIoT ecosystems. It explores AIoT architectures spanning devices, edge, fog, and cloud computing, along with smart sensors, embedded systems, intelligent actuators, communication technologies including 5G, 6G, LoRaWAN, NB-IoT, and Wi-Fi 7. The chapter further discusses Edge AI, TinyML, digital twins, AIoT development platforms, and concludes with a practical case study on smart city infrastructure. Chapter 2 focuses on intelligent data analytics and AI models that power connected systems. It explains sensor data acquisition, feature engineering, machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, natural language processing, reinforcement learning, explainable AI, federated learning, and privacy-preserving intelligence. The chapter concludes with a real-world AIoT healthcare case study demonstrating predictive healthcare and remote patient monitoring. Chapter 3 explores advanced AI computing paradigms that enable autonomous intelligent systems. Topics include distributed edge intelligence, TinyML, Generative AI, Agentic AI, Large Language Models (LLMs), collaborative multi-agent systems, digital twins, intelligent robotics, human-robot collaboration, and cyber-physical systems. The chapter concludes with an Industry 5.0 smart manufacturing case study illustrating AI-driven industrial automation. Chapter 4 addresses one of the most critical aspects of AIoT—security, resilience, sustainability, and governance. It presents AIoT security architectures, Zero Trust frameworks, AI-driven intrusion detection, blockchain-enabled security, identity and access management, confidential AI, secure edge computing, green AIoT technologies, smart energy systems, AI governance, responsible AI, and regulatory compliance. A comprehensive case study demonstrates AIoT security solutions for critical infrastructure protection. Chapter 5 presents emerging technologies and future innovations shaping intelligent AIoT ecosystems. The chapter discusses foundation models, LLM-driven automation, quantum AI, quantum machine learning, AIoT applications in healthcare, agriculture, transportation, smart campuses, defense, environmental sustainability, space technologies, and disaster management. It also explores future research directions including 6G AIoT, neuromorphic computing, swarm intelligence, and cognitive edge computing. The chapter concludes with a capstone project that integrates the knowledge acquired throughout the book into the design and deployment of a complete intelligent AIoT system. One of the distinguishing strengths of this book is its emphasis on engineering-oriented learning. Each chapter integrates conceptual discussions with practical applications, industrial use cases, architecture diagrams, emerging research topics, and case studies that bridge the gap between academic knowledge and real-world implementation. The inclusion of recent advancements such as Generative AI, Large Language Models, Explainable AI, Federated Learning, TinyML, Digital Twins, Quantum AI, Physical AI, Agentic AI, and Responsible AI ensures that readers remain aligned with current technological developments and future industrial requirements. This book has been written with the objective of serving as a comprehensive textbook for undergraduate and postgraduate engineering programs, a valuable reference for research scholars, and a practical guide for professionals working in artificial intelligence, IoT, cloud computing, cybersecurity, data science, embedded systems, robotics, and intelligent automation. The content has been prepared in a structured and accessible manner to support classroom teaching, self-learning, laboratory activities, research projects, industrial training, and innovation-driven product development. As a collaborative effort by multiple authors with diverse academic, research, and industrial expertise, this book reflects a multidisciplinary perspective on intelligent AIoT systems. The combined experiences of the authors have contributed to creating a resource that balances theoretical depth with practical relevance while addressing contemporary challenges and future opportunities in intelligent connected technologies. The authors express their sincere gratitude to their respective institutions, colleagues, researchers, students, industry collaborators, reviewers, and family members whose encouragement, constructive feedback, and continuous support made this publication possible. We also acknowledge the contributions of the global scientific community whose research and innovations continue to advance the fields of Artificial Intelligence, Internet of Things, edge computing, cloud computing, cybersecurity, intelligent automation, and sustainable digital transformation. It is our sincere hope that Engineering Intelligent AIoT Systems: Artificial Intelligence for Smart Connected Technologies will inspire readers to explore innovative ideas, develop intelligent engineering solutions, conduct impactful research, and contribute meaningfully to the advancement of smart connected technologies that benefit society, industry, and the global digital economy.

title: Quantum computing-enhanced deep learning for real-time detection and mitigation of cyberattack patterns
abstract: Cyberattacks are increasing in sophistication. As a result, traditional cybersecurity systems based on classical computing and conventional deep-learning techniques are increasingly exhibiting limitations and vulnerabilities. Although deep-learning models offer substantial advantages over traditional methods for automated intrusion detection through large-scale security data analysis and pattern recognition, they suffer from notable constraints related to high-dimensional feature spaces, scalability, and stringent real-time inference requirements. This work proposes a quantum-enhanced deep learning (QEDL) framework for detecting and mitigating real-time cyberattack patterns. Quantum computing technologies—specifically quantum feature selection and quantum data encoding—are integrated into a classical–hybrid quantum deep-learning architecture. The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) is employed for quantum feature selection to enable efficient identification of discriminative features from high-dimensional cybersecurity datasets. In addition, quantum data encoding exploits superposition and entanglement to process multiple complex inputs simultaneously. The resulting quantum feature representations are processed using parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs), followed by classical deep-learning layers for accurate threat classification. The proposed QEDL framework is evaluated using the CIC–IDS2017 dataset, and its performance is compared against classical deep-learning models and pure quantum neural networks. Experimental results demonstrate that, within the proposed hybrid quantum–classical framework, the QAOA-based feature selection strategy achieved higher classification performance than the evaluated classical feature selection methods under the reported experimental settings. In addition, the proposed framework exhibited improved generalization to previously unseen attacks. These findings suggest that the proposed hybrid quantum–classical framework is a promising approach for cyberattack detection under the experimental conditions considered in this study. The experiments in this study were simulated using IBM Aer backend, without physical quantum hardware. The results obtained in this study serve as a simulation-based proof of concept.

title: Quantum AI for Cybersecurity: A hybrid Quantum-Classical models for attack path analysis
abstract: Modern cyberattacks are increasingly complex, posing significant challenges to classical machine learning methods, particularly when labeled data is limited and feature interactions are highly non-linear. In this study we investigates the potential of hybrid quantum-classical learning to enhance feature representations for intrusion detection and explore possible quantum advantages in cybersecurity analytics. Using the UNSW-NB15 dataset, network traffic is transformed into structured feature vectors through classical preprocessing and normalization. Classical models, including Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machines with linear and RBF kernels, are evaluated on the full dataset to establish baseline performance under large-sample conditions. Simultaneously, a quantum-enhanced pipeline maps classical features into variational quantum circuits via angle encoding and entangling layers, executed on a CPU-based quantum simulator, with resulting quantum embeddings classified using a classical SVM. Experiments show that while classical models achieve higher overall accuracy with large datasets, quantum-enhanced representations demonstrate superior attack recall and improved class separability when data is scarce, suggesting that quantum feature spaces capture complex correlations inaccessible to shallow classical models. These results highlight the potential of quantum embeddings to improve generalization and representation quality in cybersecurity tasks and provide a reproducible framework for evaluating quantum advantages as quantum hardware and simulators continue to advance.

title: Quantum computing in image recognition: A comparative analysis with classical models
abstract: This research explores quantum machine learning for image classification, comparing classical and quantum models. A classical convolutional neural network (CNN), based on the LeNet architecture, achieved 99.12% accuracy on MNIST, outperforming a quantum CNN, which attained 93.30%. Quantum encoders applied to Fashion-MNIST reached 85.60%, while quantum support vector machine (SVM), implemented for binary classification, obtained 71.34%. The study integrates hybrid quantum-classical models, leveraging quantum circuits for feature extraction. A quantum autoencoder-based classifier was introduced, demonstrating efficient data compression and classification without additional qubits. Feature encoding using RX gates mapped classical data into quantum states, and the impact of parameterized quantum circuit structures on classification accuracy was analyzed. Results indicate that specific ansatz structures yield superior accuracy, highlighting the significance of quantum circuit design. While classical models currently outperform quantum counterparts, quantum approaches reduce trainable parameters and computational complexity. Limitations in current quantum hardware, including noise and scalability, restrict performance. However, advancements in error mitigation, quantum gate efficiency, and scalable quantum architecture could bridge the gap with classical methods. These quantum techniques hold potential in aerospace applications, such as satellite image classification, anomaly detection in remote sensing, and real-time processing of high-dimensional image data. This study underscores the growing role of quantum circuits in machine learning, particularly in feature extraction and classification, suggesting that future quantum hardware could unlock new capabilities in end-to-end learning beyond hybrid approaches.

title: Adversarially Robust QSL on UNSW-NB15 experiment
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This repository provides the reproducibility package for a controlled study of adversarial robustness in quantum supervised learning (QSL) for network intrusion detection using the UNSW-NB15 benchmark. The experiment evaluates a four-qubit variational QSL intrusion detector together with a matched classical multilayer perceptron (MLP) baseline. The shared preprocessing pipeline applies categorical encoding, feature extraction, principal component analysis to four dimensions, and scaling to the interval [0, π]. Experiments are conducted over ten matched random seeds. White-box Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) and Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) attacks are evaluated at perturbation budgets ε/π = 0.02, 0.05, and 0.10. The robust QSL training protocol uses a mixture of 50% clean, 25% FGSM, and 25% PGD samples. PGD uses three steps during adversarial training and seven steps during final evaluation. The repository contains the principal experiment notebooks, repeated-seed robustness results, attack diagnostics, statistical summaries, confidence intervals, paired statistical tests, effect-size analyses, and quantum-versus-classical comparison outputs. Across ten matched seeds, PGD-aware adversarial training improves QSL accuracy from 9.10% to 26.90% under PGD at ε = 0.05π and from 2.60% to 20.73% at ε = 0.10π. This improvement is accompanied by a reduction in clean QSL accuracy from 70.73% to 61.57%. The adversarially trained classical MLP retains higher absolute robustness, achieving 64.27% and 50.50% accuracy at PGD 0.05π and 0.10π, respectively. These results demonstrate that PGD-aware adversarial training materially strengthens the evaluated QSL model but do not establish quantum advantage. The repository is intended to support transparent reproduction, independent verification, and further research on adversarial robustness in quantum machine learning for cybersecurity.

title: Assessing Absolute Distributed Data Scheduling Functions in Global Grid-Based Cloud Computing
abstract: In global grid-based cloud computing settings, performance optimization depends on effective data scheduling. The usefulness of the absolute distributed data scheduling function in controlling resource allocation, load balancing, and data dissemination across heterogeneous cloud infrastructures is assessed in this study. By taking into account variables including data locality, processing capacity, and network latency, we evaluate the function's capacity to increase system throughput while reducing scheduling overhead. Simulations that compare to current scheduling models show gains in fault tolerance, scalability, and efficiency. High-performance cloud computing is advanced by the findings, which offer insights on optimizing distributed scheduling systems. title: QFedAstro: Quantum-Enhanced Federated Learning with Adaptive Mission Intelligence for Astronaut Health Monitoring
abstract: Deep-space medical surveillance necessitates decentralized AI frameworks that are resilient to communication latency and resource scarcity. This study introduces QFedAstro, which integrates variational quantum circuits with federated learning for astronaut health anomaly detection across heterogeneous mission profiles. The architecture employs five synergistic modules: quantum-classical hybrid optimization (QCHO) navigating non-convex loss landscapes via superposition-inspired parameter updates; adaptive mission intelligence networks (AMIN) reconfiguring layer weights based on gravity-radiation-isolation vectors; temporal-spatial health embedding (TSHE) capturing physiological interdependencies through graph attention; privacy-preserving biometric fusion (PPBF) applying mission-calibrated differential noise (ϵ = 0.5, δ = 10 -5 ); and cross-mission knowledge crystallization (CMKC) enabling inter-environment transfer learning. Validation across 150-astronaut simulations spanning ISS, Lunar, Martian, and Deep Space contexts yields 96.73% accuracy—2.61% above centralized baselines—while achieving 147x privacy amplification and 68% bandwidth reduction. Paired t-tests confirmed significance (p < 0.001, Cohen’s d = 2.41). The framework challenges conventional privacy-utility tradeoffs, demonstrating that quantum augmentation enables the concurrent optimization of fidelity and sovereignty in mission-critical federated systems.

title: Recent Advances in Secure Medical Image Cryptanalysis with Quantum Neural Networks for IoT-Enabled Cloud Storage: A Systematic Review
venue: International Journal on Advanced Computer Theory and Engineering
abstract: The rapid growth of IoT-enabled healthcare systems and cloud storage technologies has significantly increased the reliance on digital medical imaging for diagnosis and treatment. However, the storage and transmission of medical images over cloud platforms introduce serious security and privacy concerns, particularly due to cyberattacks, data breaches, and adversarial manipulations. Medical images, including MRI, CT, and X-ray scans, contain sensitive patient information that must be protected during storage and communication. Traditional cryptographic techniques, while effective, are increasingly vulnerable to emerging threats, especially with the advent of quantum computing. Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) have opened new possibilities for secure medical image cryptanalysis and protection. Deep learning-based cryptographic techniques have demonstrated the ability to enhance image encryption, authentication, and secure transmission while maintaining diagnostic quality. Additionally, quantum computing introduces advanced cryptographic paradigms such as Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) and quantum-enhanced encryption, which significantly improve data security in IoT-enabled cloud environments. Quantum neural networks further enhance cryptographic systems by enabling efficient processing of high-dimensional medical image data while ensuring privacy preservation through quantum cryptography mechanisms. Moreover, recent studies highlight that adversarial attacks on AI-based medical imaging systems can lead to incorrect diagnoses, emphasizing the need for robust and secure architectures. This paper presents a comprehensive systematic review of recent advances in secure medical image cryptanalysis using quantum neural networks in IoT-enabled cloud storage systems. It examines AI-driven cryptographic techniques, quantum-based security models, and hybrid frameworks, while identifying research trends, challenges, and future directions for developing secure and efficient healthcare systems.

title: HyQCAN: A Quantum-Classical Synergy for Secure and Low-Latency Emergency Communication in Vehicular Ad Hoc Networks
abstract: Connected Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) are poised to revolutionize intelligent transportation by enhancing road safety and reducing traffic congestion through real-time communication. However, this dependency introduces vulnerabilities to cyberattacks, especially in emergency scenarios where secure, low-latency communication is critical. While Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) provides quantum-secure key exchange, relying solely on it for all communication processes can introduce latency during key generation, which can be problematic in time-sensitive situations. To address this, we propose HyQCAN, a Hybrid Quantum-Classical Authentication Network that integrates QKD with Dynamic Basis Switching (DBS) for vehicle identity authentication of emergency vehicles in Vehicular Ad Hoc Networks (VANETs). QKD ensures quantum-secure encryption, while DBS enables real-time adaptation of the key exchange process based on communication urgency. HyQCAN achieves an optimal balance between security and responsiveness, with an Average Authentication Time (AAT) of 3.34 ms and an Average Key Generation Efficiency (AKGE) of 111.82 bps, effectively safeguarding critical VANET communications in high-priority situations.

The multidisciplinary partnership includes BT, the National Physical Laboratory, and academic institutions such as Loughborough University, University of Bristol, and King’s College London. Together, they bring a comprehensive lens to assurance: from physical layer vulnerabilities and side-channel risks to protocol compliance, post-processing evaluation, and supply chain integrity. This adversarial approach not only challenges the status quo but also drives faster, more robust assurance practices—helping pave the way for trustworthy quantum-secure networks. title: Quantum Gated Recurrent GAN with Gaussian Uncertainty for Network Anomaly Detection
abstract: Anomaly detection in time-series data is a critical challenge with significant implications for network security. Recent quantum machine learning approaches, such as quantum kernel methods and variational quantum circuits, have shown promise in capturing complex data distributions for anomaly detection but remain constrained by limited qubit counts. We introduce in this work a novel Quantum Gated Recurrent Unit (QGRU)-based Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) employing Successive Data Injection (SuDaI) and a multi-metric gating strategy for robust network anomaly detection. Our model uniquely utilizes a quantum-enhanced generator that outputs parameters (mean and log-variance) of a Gaussian distribution via reparameterization, combined with a Wasserstein critic to stabilize adversarial training. Anomalies are identified through a novel gating mechanism that initially flags potential anomalies based on Gaussian uncertainty estimates and subsequently verifies them using a composite of critic scores and reconstruction errors. Evaluated on benchmark datasets, our method achieves a high time-series aware F1 score (TaF1) of 89.43% demonstrating superior capability in detecting anomalies accurately and promptly as compared to existing classical and quantum models. Furthermore, the trained QGRU-WGAN was deployed on real IBM Quantum hardware, where it retained high anomaly detection performance, confirming its robustness and practical feasibility on current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices.

title: Evaluating the Potential of Quantum Machine Learning in Cybersecurity: A Case-Study on PCA-based Intrusion Detection Systems
abstract: Quantum computing promises to revolutionize our understanding of the limits of computation, and its implications in cryptography have long been evident. Today, cryptographers are actively devising post-quantum solutions to counter the threats posed by quantum-enabled adversaries. Meanwhile, quantum scientists are innovating quantum protocols to empower defenders. However, the broader impact of quantum computing and quantum machine learning (QML) on other cybersecurity domains still needs to be explored. In this work, we investigate the potential impact of QML on cybersecurity applications of traditional ML. First, we explore the potential advantages of quantum computing in machine learning problems specifically related to cybersecurity. Then, we describe a methodology to quantify the future impact of fault-tolerant QML algorithms on real-world problems. As a case study, we apply our approach to standard methods and datasets in network intrusion detection, one of the most studied applications of machine learning in cybersecurity. Our results provide insight into the conditions for obtaining a quantum advantage and the need for future quantum hardware and software advancements.
