This robust approach enables practical phase control in entangled-photon systems and can be extended to time-bin QKD via time–polarization mapping, offering a promising route toward stable, low-QBER quantum communication.

title: A Mathematically Proven and Secure Quantum Key Distribution System with Adaptive Error Correction and Privacy Amplification (AWEM-QKD)
abstract: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols offer unparalleled security by leveraging the laws of quantum mechanics. However, standard protocols like BB84 and E91 face challenges when quantum channel noise increases and eavesdropping remains undetected under fixed logic gates. This paper introduces a novel adaptive approach-AWEM-QKD-which integrates Quantum Adaptive Hadamard (QAH), Quantum Conditional Entanglement Logic (QCEL), and Adaptive Measurement Validation Logic (AMVL). These logics dynamically optimize gate behavior, reduce error rates, and strengthen resistance against quantum attacks. This system is mathematically proven, algorithmically structured, and supported by circuit simulation. Comparative analysis with traditional systems highlights improved efficiency, QBER reduction, and detection accuracy, thus making AWEM-QKD highly suitable for secure quantum communications.

title: Stealthy Low Earth Orbit Satellite-To-Ground Quantum Communication
venue: DROPS (Schloss Dagstuhl – Leibniz Center for Informatics)
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) leveraging satellites holds promise for global-scale secure communication. However, its practical deployment is threatened by the inherent predictability of satellite orbits, which exposes quantum channels to targeted eavesdropping attacks, compromising the physical-layer security guarantees of QKD. Through security analysis, we demonstrate that such attacks can drastically increase the quantum bit error rate (QBER) from 4.7% to 27.5%, effectively disrupting secure key generation. To address this fundamental vulnerability, we introduce a novel defense framework that integrates two strategies: (1) Stealthy Deployment, which obfuscates quantum satellites within massive LEO constellations to drastically increase an adversary’s search space, and (2) Dynamic Re-routing, which is an adaptive countermeasure that re-establishes QKD sessions via alternative paths upon eavesdropping detection. Evaluated through large-scale simulations incorporating real-world satellite data, our framework demonstrates up to a 90% improvement in key generation rate under active attack, ensuring robust and resilient satellite-based QKD without modifications to the underlying quantum hardware.

title: Development of Quantum Key Distribution: Cybersecurity Data Transfer over Dispersed Classical and Quantum Computing Nodes
abstract: Traditional cryptographic methods are becoming more and more vulnerable when facing the computing power delivered by the quantum algorithm in the era of digitalization heading towards quantum computing. The realization of a quantum computer is a growing menace that has promoted the development of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), a completely secure key exchange protocol based on the principles of quantum mechanics. This work studies QKD protocol creation and use for secure data transfer in hybrid networks including both classical and quantum computing nodes over geographically separated environments. The paper provides a scalable scheme to integrate QKD with current classical communication networks, with the emphasis on interoperability, key synchronization, secure routing among the mixed nodes. At the core of the model are quantum channels for key exchange and classical channels for data, governed by a quantum-safe control protocol. The security of QKD—the feature of resistance against eavesdropping according to the no-cloning theorem and disturbance of measurement—is investigated taking into account actual implementation aspects, such as noise, restriction in a transmission distance, and quantum memory. To test the model, simulation, and prototype testing are performed over different networking topologies, considering various parameters such as QBER, key generation rate, latency and system robustness under different attacks such as man-in-the-middle as well as photon-number-splitting attacks. We also investigate the interworking between QKD and post-quantum cryptography (PQC) to reduce the risk for hybrid systems with enhanced security and to be backward compatible to classical systems. Findings show that, when well combined with classical and quantum computing nodes, QKD is able to bring the cybersecurity of today communication infrastructures to a greater extent. This research is a step towards building the quantum internet, providing a solid foundation for applications in cybersecurity and potentially well beyond — finance, defense, health care and more — where data privacy truly matters.

title: BB84 Quantum Key Distribution in Software‐Defined Networking Control Planes: End‐to‐End Integration, Security Analysis, and Performance Benchmarking
abstract: ABSTRACT Classical public‐key cryptography used to secure Software‐Defined Networking (SDN) control planes remains vulnerable to future cryptographically relevant quantum computers through Shor's algorithm, motivating the exploration of quantum‐safe key establishment mechanisms. While Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) has been widely studied as a standalone technology, its direct integration into SDN control‐plane protection remains insufficiently quantified from both architectural and operational perspectives. This paper presents a quantum‐secure SDN control‐plane framework in which BB84‐based key generation, key lifecycle management, and quantum‐authenticated flow‐rule protection are integrated into the Ryu controller through a QBER‐aware Key Management System (KMS) and OpenFlow 1.3 Experimenter extensions. Beyond implementation, the paper positions the design as a practical migration model for quantum‐resilient SDN infrastructures and evaluates its security–performance trade‐offs against a classical RSA + TLS baseline. The system is implemented using Ryu, Open vSwitch, and a software BB84 simulator in a Mininet testbed with up to 20 OpenFlow switches. All measurements are repeated over 30 independent trials with full statistical reporting, while QBER stability is assessed over 1000 runs. Results show that BB84 key generation latency averages 45.3 ms ( σ = 3.2 ms), mean QBER remains at 4.8% with zero threshold violations, flow installation latency increases from 13.2 to 17.6 ms, controller CPU overhead is +3.8 percentage points, and throughput decreases from 8200 to 7580 pps under saturation. In addition, scalability follows a near‐perfect linear trend ( R 2 = 0.998), enabling projection to larger SDN deployments. These findings show that QKD‐secured SDN control‐plane protection is operationally feasible on commodity hardware with bounded and predictable overhead, while offering a practical blueprint for the gradual deployment of quantum‐resilient networking infrastructure.

title: Characterization of QBER contributions of phase-encoding QKD transmitters with an optical coherent receiver
abstract: The technological development of QKD (Quantum Key Distribution) is accelerating from a research topic towards commercial deployment. QKD initiatives are increasingly addressing real-world use cases. Besides lots of literature on theory and lab-demos, first high Technology-Readiness Level systems are available. Due to the security guarantees it has to provide, the performance of any QKD implementation is particularly sensitive to any imperfections that may lead to an increase of the QBER (Quantum Bit Error Rate). Achieving high performance, or a low QBER value, constitutes a challenging engineering task, as the operating systems need to be highly optimized in many aspects. In particular, accurate phase modulation is the foundation of high system performance in case of phase-encoding protocols. In most cases, the overall QBER is measured with a QKD receiver, which accumulates errors from transmitter, quantum channel and receiver. This requires an operational transmitter system and additionally prevents the investigation of the pure transmitter output signal’s characteristics. However, for support of transmitter integration and test activities as well as for validation tasks, a more suitable method remains to be developed. In this paper, we propose such a method by making use of a coherent receiver. This device provides extended signal information including the signal amplitude and its current relative phase. Therefore, it is possible to monitor phase-encoding correctness and precision, among other relevant signal properties. We analyze the reasonability of using a coherent receiver, by outlining its capabilites to measure QBER contributors occurring in a given basic reference QKD transmitter system. Our findings indicate that employing a coherent receiver is a simple method to accelerate development and validation of phase-encoding QKD transmitter systems.

title: Effective Quantum Bit Error Rate Reduction in Frequency-Encoded Quantum Key Distribution Using Hong-Ou-Mandel Interference
abstract: We experimentally demonstrate a practical method for suppressing inter-bin crosstalk in frequency-bin-encoded quantum key distribution using Hong-Ou-Mandel interference, largely reducing the quantum bit error rate (QBER) from 3.8% to 0.34% and improving overall system performance.

title: AWEM-QKD: Quadratically Accelerating Finite-Key Security in Quantum Key Distribution via Adaptive Logic-Layer Error Mitigation
abstract: AWEM-QKD (Adaptive Window Error Mitigation Quantum Key Distribution) is a novel quantum cryptographic framework designed to address one of the most significant barriers to practical quantum key distribution (QKD): finite-key security limitations. Existing QKD systems require large numbers of exchanged quantum signals before provable secrecy can be established, resulting in increased latency, reduced photon efficiency, and scalability challenges. This research introduces an adaptive logic-layer error mitigation mechanism that operates on structured sliding windows of measurement outcomes prior to privacy amplification. Unlike conventional approaches that primarily rely on error correction and reconciliation after measurement, AWEM-QKD proactively stabilizes measurement outcomes while preserving entropy. By reducing effective quantum bit error rate (QBER), the protocol increases mutual information between legitimate users and improves the asymptotic secret key rate. The research develops a rigorous information-theoretic framework based on binary entropy, mutual information, the Devetak–Winter bound, finite-key composable security, and adversarial information analysis. A key theoretical contribution is the derivation and validation of a quadratic scaling relationship demonstrating that increases in asymptotic secret key rate result in substantial reductions in the minimum secure block size required for finite-key security certification. Simulation-based evaluation under realistic noise conditions demonstrates: Reduction of effective QBER through adaptive window-based mitigation. Improvement in mutual information between communicating parties. Increased asymptotic secret key rates. Faster convergence to the secure regime. Significant reduction in minimum secure block size requirements. Enhanced practicality of quantum-secure communications in resource-constrained environments. The proposed architecture operates entirely at the logical processing layer and can be integrated with existing QKD implementations without requiring modifications to quantum hardware. The research contributes a scalable and deployable pathway toward low-latency, high-throughput, and secure next-generation quantum communication systems.

title: Security‐Enhanced Differential Binary‐Phase‐Shift‐Keying Quantum Key Distribution With a Wavelength‐Switchable Single‐Photon Carrier
abstract: A single‐chip dual‐wavelength coherent photon source is proposed to introduce additional parametric uncertainty and improve the security scaling of single‐photon differential binary‐phase‐shift‐keying quantum key distribution (D‐BPSK‐QKD). Simultaneous lasing of two longitudinal modes in the same semiconductor laser cavity generates two coherent photon groups at different wavelengths, and attenuation of their combined output to the single‐photon level inevitably produces wavelength uncertainty at the receiver. Optical injection control enables stabilized D‐BPSK encoding on one selected mode while the other mode remains free‐running, which supports mode‐selective coding and a decoy scenario during single‐photon streaming. This intermodal wavelength switching/selection provides another degree of freedom for QKD security and increases the difficulty of eavesdropping attacks. The dual‐wavelength single‐photon bits deliver D‐BPSK‐QKD codes with a QBER of <4.1% under 2 10 ‐bit encryption, a sifted key rate of 408.6 kbit/s, and a secure key rate (SKR) of 10.5 kbit/s at an average photon number of 0.22 photons#/bit. The transmission distance can be extended to more than 13.25 km with a SKR of 3.6 kbit/s under a nearly equivalent QBER. This versatile wavelength‐uncertain coding or decoying operation enables flexible and secure D‐BPSK‐QKD transmission over wavelength‐division‐multiplexed channelized single‐mode fiber links.

title: Quantum Key Distribution Secured Federated Learning for Channel Estimation and Radar Spectrum Sensing in 6G Networks
abstract: This paper presents a federated learning framework secured by quantum key distribution (QKD) for wireless channel estimation and radar spectrum sensing in the next generation networks (NextG or Beyond 6G). A BB84-style protocol abstraction and pairwise additive masking are utilized to train clients' local models (CNN for channel estimation, U-Net for radar segmentation) and upload only masked model updates. The server aggregates without observing plain parameters; an eavesdropper without QKD keys cannot recover individual updates. Experiments show that secure FL achieves NMSE of 0.216 for channel estimation and 92.1\% accuracy with 0.72 mIoU for radar sensing. When an eavesdropper is present, QBER rises to $\sim$25\% and all rounds abort as intended; reconstruction error remains below $10^{-5}$, confirming correct aggregation.

title: Adaptive Quantum-Integrated Access Control Mechanism for Protecting LoRaWAN Against Emerging Quantum Threats
venue: International Conference on Pervasive Computing and Social Networking (ICPCSN)
abstract: As the Internet of Things (IoT) continues to expand rapidly, securing authentication and key exchange in Low-Power Wide-Area-Networks (LPWANs) like LoRaWAN has become increasingly critical. With the advent of quantum computing, traditional cryptographic techniques face significant threats, necessitating the exploration of quantum-resistant solutions. This research proposes a novel security mechanism that integrates Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) into the LoRaWAN to enhance device authentication. Since we don’t have real hardware, we have done simulation-based experiments. The simulation was implemented in Python using QuTiP [Quantum Toolbox] for quantum state modeling, NumPy for random generation [qubits], & Matplotlib for visualization. The experiment is designed to compare the security robustness of LoRaWAN Device-Join attempts in 3 scenarios: 1. Quantum attack on LoRaWAN Key Exchange Process in the existing framework, 2. Key exchange without eavesdropper in the proposed framework, & 3. Key exchange with the presence of eavesdropper in the proposed framework. The experiment involves encoding qubits in diagonal bases and transmitting them between parties. An intercept-resend attack is modeled to simulate eavesdropping and the protocol includes key reconciliation through basis comparison. The Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) is calculated to evaluate the integrity of the exchanged key, with a predefined threshold determining whether to accept or reject a device's join request. Over 50 simulation trials, and results, this proposed framework consistently demonstrated high rejection rates in the presence of eavesdropping; indicating its effectiveness in detecting and preventing unauthorized access. By embedding QKD into the LoRaWAN device-join process, this proposed approach establishes a secure, quantum-resilient foundation for authentication in resource-constrained IoT environments, effectively addressing the security challenges posed by the quantum era.

title: Implementation of a Quantum Authentication Protocol Using Single Photons in Deployed Fiber
abstract: With the increasing importance of securing quantum communication networks, practical and robust entity authentication is a critical requirement. Accordingly, we propose and experimentally validate a quantum entity authentication (QEA) protocol specifically designed for integration with BB84-type quantum key distribution (QKD) workflows and existing terminal architectures. We analyze the protocol's security against intercept-resend man-in-the-middle (MitM) impersonation, showing that an unauthenticated adversary induces a characteristic 25% correlation error and that the rejection probability approaches unity as the number of detected authentication events increases. For practical realization, the protocol is deployed using weak coherent pulses (WCPs) with decoy-state estimation to bound single-photon contributions and mitigate photon-number-splitting (PNS)-enabled leakage. The system is demonstrated over a field-deployed fiber link of approximately 20 km with ~8 dB optical loss using signal/decoy intensities of ~0.5/~0.15 and sending probabilities 0.88/0.10/0.02 (signal/decoy/vacuum). Across both verification directions, stable operation is observed with quantum bit error rate (QBER) typically fluctuating between 1% and 4% while the sifted key rate remains constant over time. These results provide an experimental basis for integrating physical-layer entity authentication into deployed quantum communication networks.

title: Improving the Performance of Free Space Quantum Communication with Adaptive Optics and Modulation Schemes
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is a promising technology for secure communication, using quantum physics concepts to encrypt information.The present study examines the effects of modulation schemes and adaptive optics (AO) on the QKD system performance over a variable link distance upto 100 km.AO is implemented to mitigate turbulence effects, while various modulation schemes are tested to improve the system performance for varying link ranges and atmospheric conditions.To check the system performance: transmittance, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and quantum bit error rate (QBER) are evaluated.The study found that AO significantly improved transmittance and SNR, particularly over longer distances.Binary Phase Shift Keying (BPSK) modulation demonstrated superior performance in terms of QBER compared to other digital modulation schemes, indicating its efficacy in enhancing data security and transmission reliability.

title: Orthogonal-state-based Measurement Device Independent Quantum Communication
abstract: We attempt to propose the first orthogonal-state-based protocols of measurement-device-independent quantum secure direct communication and quantum dialogue employing single basis, i.e., Bell basis as decoy qubits for eavesdropping detection. Orthogonal-state-based protocols are inherently distinct from conventional conjugate-coding protocols, offering unconditional security derived from the duality and monogamy of entanglement. Notably, these orthogonal-state-based protocols demonstrate improved performance over conjugate-coding based protocols under certain noisy environments, highlighting the significance of selecting the best basis choice of decoy qubits for secure quantum communication under collective noise. Furthermore, we rigorously analyze the security of the proposed protocols against various eavesdropping strategies, including intercept-and-resend attack, entangle-and-measure attack, information leakage attack, flip attack, and disturbance or modification attack. Our findings also show that, with appropriate modifications, the proposed orthogonal-state-based measurement-device-independent quantum secure direct communication protocol can be transformed into orthogonal-state-based measurement-device-independent versions of quantum key distribution protocols, expanding their applicability. Our protocols leverage fundamentally distinct resources to close the security loopholes linked to measurement devices, while also effectively doubling the distance for secure direct message transmission compared to traditional quantum communication methods.

title: Quantum Networking: Information Encoding and Decoding Strategies
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper investigates optimal information encoding and decoding strategies within quantum networks. The core aim is to enhance information transmission efficiency and security by leveraging principles from information theory and quantum information theory. We analyze various encoding and decoding schemes, quantifying their performance using key metrics such as channel capacity and quantum bit error rate (QBER). This work focuses on identifying strategies that maximize the fidelity of quantum information transfer, considering the inherent challenges posed by quantum noise and decoherence. The proposed strategies incorporate adaptive coding techniques and error correction protocols tailored to specific network topologies and noise characteristics. Ultimately, this research contributes to the development of more robust and efficient quantum networks, a critical component of future quantum communication systems.

title: Early Warning from the Recovery Speed of a Pointing-and-Tracking Loop in Free-Space Quantum Key Distribution: A Concept Note on the Readings Required
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: India has demonstrated its first free-space quantum key distribution (QKD) link, 5.56 km long, with a pointing, acquisition and tracking (PAT) system holding the quantum channel on target, a quantum bit error rate (QBER) below 5% and a secure key rate of 230–260 bits per second. Longer and satellite-relevant links make pointing harder. This note proposes a small, fixed, training-free calculation that runs on the tracking loop’s own residual, the small error it corrects many times a second. In a healthy link each nudge is corrected quickly. As pointing starts to drift, the correction settles more slowly, and this can show before the QBER rises. A graded response, limited to the entities of the ground terminal, can then begin early. The note names an assumed set of readings, shows how the calculation uses them, and lists the data afirst test would need. It makes no claim about the inside of any particular system.

title: Polarization-Maintaining Fiber Alignment Requirements for Quantum Communication
abstract: When polarization-maintaining fiber is used in quantum communication, axis alternation of successive fiber segments can compensate for differential group delay. To minimize the QBER of transmitted signals, the requirements on fiber segment accuracy are computed.

title: Quantum Network Key Distribution Protocol Topological Optimization
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper investigates the optimization of topological structures within quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols. The core claim is that strategic topological optimization can significantly enhance key distribution efficiency and security. The proposed methodology leverages analytical analysis of quantum network topologies to identify optimal key distribution schemes. Specifically, we explore how the arrangement of nodes and connections within a quantum network impacts the performance of protocols like BB84 and E91. The underlying mechanism involves utilizing the inherent properties of quantum entanglement to achieve highly efficient and secure key exchange. We present a framework for evaluating different topological configurations based on metrics such as key generation rate, channel loss, and eavesdropping detection probability. The results demonstrate a clear correlation between optimized topologies and improved QKD performance. Furthermore, we address the challenges associated with implementing these optimized topologies, including considerations for quantum repeater placement and network scalability. This research contributes to the advancement of practical QKD systems by providing a rigorous approach to topological design.

title: Enhanced Quantum Key Distribution and Error Minimization for 6G Networks through Optimized Multi-Head Self-Attention and Gated-Dilated Convolutional Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract 6G frameworks will be able to utilize higher frequencies than 5G frameworks and provide altogether higher capacity and much lower latency. First, 6G network input signals stand up to channel obstacles to open security. QKD, a cryptographic technique, allows two parties to safely exchange secret keys for message encryption and decryption. Based on quantum mechanics, any threats in the system warn the authorized users. Qubits can be distributed over fibre or free space quantum channels and encoded with several degrees of freedom. In this proposed method, QKD and Error Rate Optimization using an optimized Multi-Head Self-Attention and Gated-Dilated Convolutional Neural Network (QKD-ERO-MSGCNN) are used to extend the maximum transmission distance and improve the secret key rate (SKR). The variable velocity strategy particle swarm optimization algorithm (VVSPSOA) is used on the input signals to improve the SKR and is fed to the MSGCNN to analyse the quantum bit error rate (QBER) reduction effectively. MSGCNN alone does not optimize the QBER reduction in the channel accurately; intensified sand cat swarm optimization (ISCSO) is used to analyse the QBER reduction accurately. The proposed QKD-ERO-MSGCNN is implemented, and metrics such as accuracy, precision, SKR and QBER reduction attain higher performances when compared with existing techniques.

title: Quantum Computing in Secure Communication: Challenges, Techniques, and Future Directions
abstract: The emergence of quantum computing has introduced both opportunities and threats to modern secure communication systems. Classical cryptographic algorithms, which rely on computational complexity, are vulnerable to quantum algorithms capable of solving problems such as integer factorization and discrete logarithms efficiently. This paper explores the role of quantum computing in secure communication, focusing on quantum cryptographic techniques such as Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) and Quantum Secure Direct Communication (QSDC). A comprehensive review of existing literature is presented, followed by an analysis of methodologies used in quantum-secure communication systems. The study evaluates the advantages, limitations, and practical challenges of implementing quantum communication technologies. Finally, future research directions and the integration of quantum technologies into next-generation communication networks are discussed.

title: Quantum-Resistant Networks using Post-Quantum Cryptography
venue: IEEE International Conference on Trust, Privacy and Security in Intelligent Systems and Applications (TPS-ISA)
abstract: Quantum networks rely on both quantum and classical channels for coordinated operation. Current architectures employ entanglement distribution and key exchange over quantum channels but often assume that classical communication is sufficiently secure. In practice, classical channels protected by traditional cryptography remain vulnerable to quantum adversaries, since large-scale quantum computers could break widely used public-key schemes and reduce the effective security of symmetric cryptography. This perspective presents a quantum-resistant network architecture that secures classical communication with post-quantum cryptographic techniques while supporting entanglementbased communication over quantum channels. Beyond cryptographic protection, the framework incorporates continuous monitoring of both quantum and classical layers, together with orchestration across heterogeneous infrastructures, to ensure end-to-end security. Collectively, these mechanisms provide a pathway toward scalable, robust, and secure quantum networks that remain dependable against both classical and quantum-era threats.

title: Secure Messaging & E-Voting System Using Quantum Cryptography
venue: International Conference on Emerging Research in Electronics, Computer Science and Technology (ICERECT)
abstract: The expansion of quantum computing puts classical cryptographic systems at risk, and thus there is a need for quantum-resistant solutions to secure messaging and e-voting. This paper introduces a two-in-one application developed with Flask (backend), Firebase (database), and IBM Quantum (live QKD operations), secured by the BB84 Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocol. The messaging module uses BB84 to produce unbreakable encryption keys by way of photon polarization, and the evoting system encrypts votes using quantum keys, providing end-to-end security. Firebase stores user information and anonymous votes securely, and Flask oversees serverside logic, including real-time quantum key generation through IBM Quantum’s cloud-based quantum processors. The incorporation of IBM Quantum’s Qiskit framework allows for real-time simulation and running of BB84, with error rates below 3% in quantum channel tests. Tamper-evident logs and decentralized verification are used in place of centralized databases for e-voting, which reduces fraud vulnerabilities. Real-world implementation shows that the system can scale, as Firebase supports 1,000+ concurrent users and IBM Quantum provides sub-second latency for key generation. This paper tackles weaknesses of traditional systems by combining quantum cryptography with contemporary full-stack technologies, offering a solid, deployable solution for electoral integrity and secure communication.

title: A tertiary review on quantum cryptography
abstract: Quantum computers impose an immense threat to system security. As a countermeasure, new cryptographic classes have been created to prevent these attacks. Technologies such as post-quantum cryptography and quantum cryptography. Quantum cryptography uses the principle of quantum physics to produce theoretically unbreakable security. This tertiary review selected 51 secondary studies from the Scopus database and presented bibliometric analysis, a list of the main techniques used in the field, and existing open challenges and future directions in quantum cryptography research. The results showed a prevalence of QKD over other techniques among the selected papers and stated that the field still faces many problems related to implementation cost, error correction, decoherence, key rates, communication distance, and quantum hacking.
first_author: Luiz Filipi Anderson de Sousa Moura

title: Quantum-Enhanced Cryptographic Key Exchange for Secure IoT Networks
venue: International Conference on Computing, Sciences and Communications (ICCSC)
abstract: The coupling of quantum-metering methods with cryptographic key exchanges spells out a new security paradigm model to safeguard Internet of Things (IoT) networks against rapidly changing cyberspace threats. The given assessment explains a quantum-advanced scenario that is operationally feasible and serves as a platform for quantum key distribution (QKD) along with classical post-quantum algorithms to deliver end-to-end confidentiality, integrity, and authentication features to a wide range of IoT devices. The model, by the virtue of quantum entanglement and photon polarization used in the creation of tamper-evident communication links, is invulnerable to adversarial-aided eavesdropping and computational assault methods and further offers a hybrid encryption protocol that has been demonstrated to alleviate key generation and exchange latency trade-offs - simultaneously maintaining scalability and effectiveness in resource-constrained IoT node environments. The key compromise probability is significantly lowered in the experimental results, along with the keys' entropy levels, which were generated in the pure QKD space as opposed to classicalbased RSA and ECC methods. Also, the framework investigates lightweight quantum-safe authentication techniques that can be used to establish trust at the device level. The output points to the enhanced resistance to quantum and classical attackers that can make the solutions work in real-time application IoT environments such as smart healthcare, autonomous systems, and industrial automation. Overall, the quantum-enriched model of cryptographic key exchange is next-gen IoT ecosystem to be implemented subsequently.

title: A Comprehensive Review of Quantum Scrambling as a Cryptographic Resource in Quantum Key Distribution
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This review examines the preprint by Daniel Süß titled "Quantum Scrambling as a Cryptographic Resource: From Krylov Complexity to Physical Channel Authentication," which proposes quantum scrambling in many-body quantum channels as a novel cryptographic primitive for channel authentication in quantum key distribution (QKD). Key postulates include the irreversibility of scrambling dynamics, the role of Lanczos coefficients in determining channel autocorrelation signatures, and the practical unforgeability protected by doubly exponential Poincaré recurrence times. Hypotheses center on the deterministic, measurable, and secure nature of scrambling-derived fingerprints, validated through simulations and real astrophysical data from the NANOGrav dataset. Results demonstrate high detection accuracy (AUC = 0.99) under realistic noise. Similar research in quantum chaos, Krylov complexity, and QKD security is surveyed, highlighting ongoing trends toward physics-based cryptography amid quantum threats. Algebraic interpretations frame Krylov subspaces as orthogonal bases for operator evolution, while geometric views depict scrambling as diffusive spreading in operator space. The field is advancing toward hybrid quantum-classical protocols resilient to quantum attacks, potentially revolutionizing secure communications. title: Investigating Physical-Layer and Cross-Layer Security Technologies in Modern Networks
venue: International Conference on Contemporary Computing and Informatics (IC3I)
abstract: As attacks get more sophisticated, traditional network security hole fixes don’t always work. We need advanced, all-around security solutions to protect contact and data transmission in complex settings. This study proposes a comprehensive solution. This study includes physical-layer encryption (PLE), quantum key distribution (QKD), cross-layer intrusion detection systems (IDS), machine-learning-based hazard detection, and cross-layer protocol design. PLE reduces noise and encryption by ensuring secure communication, whereas QKD increases security via coupling and key changes. To secure networks, cross-layer IDS detects borders and unusual activity. Using machine learning, systems get smarter by categorizing threats and anticipating their occurrence. To ensure interaction safety, the cross-layer protocol employs quantum entanglement, updated keys, and translations. An ablation analysis shows how important each technique is, and detailed comparison studies with tables and figures show that this combined strategy does better than traditional methods in terms of throughput, latency, encryption strength, false positive rate, accuracy of detection, energy efficiency, protocol effectiveness, security score, and the number of false positives. This novel, low-cost technology protects networks and lets systems adapt to new threats, improving speed and reliability.

title: Impact of dynamic ocean-atmosphere interface on quantum communication performance
abstract: Quantum communication at the sea-air interface is an important direction for expanding quantum information networks. However, current research has not sufficiently considered how waves and bubbles at this interface affect quantum communication. The paper develops a system combining the Cox-Munk sea surface wave model with the Hall-Novarini bubble scattering model, using Monte Carlo simulations to model photon propagation in air-sea channels. Based on data for different wind speeds (5–20 m/s) and four water types (pure, clear, coastal, harbor), the study examines how the sea-air interface influences quantum bit error rate (QBER) and received power for quantum communication. Results show that in pure seawater, higher wind speeds decrease the maximum secure communication depth from 63 m to 25 m. In waters with high turbidity, scattering effects dominate, limiting communication depth to within 10 m. This research identifies environmental thresholds for marine quantum channels, offering a theoretical basis and practical guidelines for designing and improving underwater quantum communication systems.

title: A Topology-Aware Quantum-Inspired Genetic Algorithm for Secure Quantum Communication
venue: IEEE Transactions on Green Communications and Networking
abstract: Quantum communication ensures that data remains secure from unauthorized access. Despite these advantages, this technology faces several challenges. For instance, photons can be lost when they go through channels, and there is a chance of eavesdropping, that make the system not as trustworthy, safe, and efficient. To make quantum communication systems function effectively in the real world, we need to combine advanced technologies like quantum error correction mechanisms and quantum repeaters. This work suggests a unified Quantum Inspired Genetic Algorithm (QIGA) framework that utilizes collaborative quantum repeaters to conquer the limitations of network links over distance. This study introduces a hybrid optimization topology (OT) that integrates mesh, star, and ring configurations for measurement device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) networks. This approach allows for the efficient use of resources for scalable quantum communication networks. The proposed network architecture integrates 12 user nodes, a trusted node, and a single shared quantum repeater within a hybrid topology. The repeater deployment has been designed to support links that are longer than 52 km. This design accommodates deployments on various scales, small, medium, and large, while optimizing resource usage and infrastructure costs. We evaluated the performance and security trade offs in quantum communication networks by optimizing three topologies with a QIGA: ring, ring-star, and ring-star-mesh hybrid (QIGA−OT). The optimization methodology aims to reconcile essential performance metrics, such as the Secure Key Rate (SKR), Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER), channel loss, and Merit of Quantum Efficiency (MQE). MQE functions as a metric for evaluating trades concerning security, efficiency, and cost-effectiveness within the network. This work presents a novel approach for utilizing quantum-inspired in the effective design and implementation of scalable network topologies across numerous fields of application.

title: A Computational Framework for Adaptive Circuit Selection in Noisy Quantum Communication Simulations
venue: Concurrency and Computation Practice and Experience
abstract: ABSTRACT Quantum communications and quantum key distribution (QKD) occupy a unique position at the intersection of quantum information processing, stochastic noise and distributed network control. Theoretical guarantees for the security of QKD based on quantum mechanics have been developed over the last several years. In order to effectively implement QKD, however, we must understand that practical implementations are limited by factors such as decoherence, imperfection of devices, and non‐homogeneous, varying environmental conditions of our distributed networks. These challenges require the need to develop adaptive computational frameworks that will dynamically adjust to changing levels of noise and to resource availability in order to successfully operate QKD, rather than relying on fixed configurations of protocols. The current study presents a means of adaptively selecting circuits for quantum communication simulated in a noisy environment using a high level of reproducibility in terms of computational frameworks and focuses upon workloads similar to QKD. Quantum communication can be treated as a decentralized, stochastic decision‐making process in which an adapting controller selects between a set of available quantum circuits based on observable network characteristics. Using the decoherence‐free subspace (DFS) encoding method and an entanglement‐based protocol that incorporates purification, the use of modular circuit templates has allowed for the selection of templates guided by the use of learned decision policies as opposed to a fixed protocol being predetermined. Unlike previous works applying reinforcement learning to tune fixed protocol parameters or measurement strategies Yang et al. and Xu et al., we model decoherence‐mitigation primitives—DFS and entanglement purification—as dynamically selectable circuit templates . In this sense, the agent acts on protocol structure instead of tuning parameters, to allow compositional adapting, on heterogeneous and adversarial network conditions. (This amounts to a qualitatively different and under‐explored control abstraction compared to the literature). Adaptive control utilizes a quantum reinforcement learning (QRL) based six qubit, four layer parameterized quantum circuit with 48 trainable parameters and a deep Q‐network (DQN) classical baseline. The agents notice the same three‐dimensional representation of state with channel loss, node‐specific noise and eavesdropping indicators. The framework is compared with more than 50 independent trials on a simulated 10‐node quantum network under a physically enriched noise model with depolarizing noise, collective dephasing, thermal relaxation (, ), amplitude‐damping leakage, nearest‐neighbor crosstalk–yielding non‐trivial von Neumann entropy values to be up to bits that give an in realistic physical depiction of decoherence. The reward function is explicitly decomposed into weighted components that are aligned to security‐critical (QBER, key rate, fidelity, entropy) metrics that are essential security, ensuring sensitivity to the most operationally relevant performance metrics. Numerical tests indicated that with noise models and circuit expressivity, QRL and classical DQN agents consistently perform in the same manner over reported metrics, and do not show any statistically significant difference between mean QBER ( p = 0.2037). Crucially, this result is not so much negative as it suggests a regime in which quantum policy models do not do better than classical baselines, yet, the QRL policy circuit operates within a genuinely quantum hypothesis space with nonzero entanglement entropy and active gradient‐based learning. It indicates that it is circuit expressivity, incentive strategy design and environment complexity which define quantum advantage of quantum communications activities (not only quantum resources by themselves). In this work we focus on the development of a transparent and extensible simulation pipeline in order to combine quantum circuit performance, stochastic noise modeling and learning‐informed adaptive control all within the framework of a one computing platform. It's about reproducibility, controlled benchmarking, and modular design, this investigation gives a concrete proving ground for further study in adaptive workflows, concurrency‐aware decision making and hybrid quantum‐classical control strategies employed in emerging quantum communication networks.

title: QuantumShield-IoT: A Quantum-Resilient Hybrid Framework for Secure Data Transmission Using Quantum Key Distribution, Lightweight Cryptography and Blockchain Technology
venue: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology (IJISRT)
abstract: With the growing Internet of Things (IoT), many applications like traffic management, smart cities, environment monitoring, industrial automation and healthcare have been revolutionized. As the number of resourcelimited IoT devices grows and connects with each other, security issues have become more intricate and severe, such as unauthorized access, data tampering, replay attacks, and the rise in threat from quantum computing to traditional cryptographic methods. To solve those problems, this paper proposes Quantum Shield-IoT, which is a quantum-resilient hybrid security framework that combines the Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocol of BB84 with ASCON lightweight authenticated encryption, blockchain security, and cloud computing to ensure secure end-to-end data transmission in IoT. The BB84 protocol works both to generate quantum secure cryptographic keys, and to identify eavesdropping via Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) analysis. The generated keys are used by ASCON-128 to ensure efficient data confidentiality, integrity and authentication with low computation load, which makes it suitable for resourceconstrained IoT devices. Encrypted data are securely stored in the cloud while the data integrity and traceability of the SHA-256 hash values are ensured by being stored on the blockchain, making them irretrievable. Encrypted data are stored securely in the cloud, while the data integrity and traceability of the hash value ensure irretrievable storage through the blockchain. The proposed framework was implemented using IBM Quantum Qiskit, ASCON-128, blockchain platforms and cloud storage. Experimental results show that quantum bit error rate (QBER) varies from 2.1% to 3.5% for typical communication and 24.8% for eavesdropping attempts, proving reliable QKD. ASCON encryption range was between 8.2 ms and 69.5 ms, and blockchain verification was less than 25 ms for 1,000 transactions with more than 99% of the integrity accuracy. Moreover, the framework achieved an attack detection rate higher than 97.9% in several cyberattacks and hence provided a scalable, light-weight and quantum resistant security solution for next generation IoT ecosystems.

title: Secure Medical Data Transmission Using Quantum Key Distribution and Post-Quantum Cryptography in Real-World Fiber Networks
abstract: The threat quantum computers pose to classical public-key cryptography motivates the deployment of quantum-safe communication for critical infrastructure such as healthcare, finance, and energy systems. Quantum key distribution (QKD) and post-quantum cryptography (PQC) offer complementary security guarantees, information-theoretic key exchange and quantum-resistant end-to-end authentication that can be combined in a layered architecture. Here, we demonstrate a field-deployed quantum-secure network integrating entanglement-based QKD with end-to-end PQC over 140 km of installed fiber in Thuringia, Germany, connecting a rural health kiosk to a university hospital via a trusted-node architecture comprising heterogeneous underground and aerial fiber links. Unlike conventional deployments that rely on a dedicated key management system to forward keys to applications, our architecture injects QKD keys directly into standard Linux-based VPN tunnels between adjacent nodes, while PQC secures the communication end-to-end, remaining fully compatible with existing infrastructure and software. Polarization-entangled photon pairs were generated at 810 nm and 1550 nm, with the telecom photon transmitted over deployed fiber. Active polarization stabilization and dispersion compensation preserve the entanglement and enable 22 days of continuous, fully autonomous operation, further underscoring the technological maturity of entanglement-based QKD approaches in a real-world fiber environment. Although the two deployed links were operated during separate rather than concurrent periods, the predominantly aerial link exhibited markedly greater instability, with QBER variations most strongly correlated with wind speed. The generated keys secured a telemedicine proof-of-concept without modifying existing medical systems, demonstrating a practical framework for quantum-safe critical infrastructures.

title: Back Cover: Analysis for Satellite‐Based High‐Dimensional Extended B92 and High‐Dimensional BB84 Quantum Key Distribution (Adv. Quantum Technol. 11/2024)
abstract: In article number 2400149, Arindam Dutta and co-workers study the implementation of high-dimensional quantum key distribution protocols, HD-Ext-B92 and HD-BB84, via satellite. The study modifies key rate calculations to explore variations in key rate, probability distribution, and quantum bit error rate (QBER) with respect to dimension and noise. The research examines how the average key rate changes with zenith angle and link length under different weather conditions, showing HD-BB84's superior performance in higher dimensions despite higher QBER saturation. The down-link configuration is shown to be preferable over the up-link configuration.

title: A scalable quantum communication framework with adaptive entanglement and QNN-based noise mitigation for secure IoT Networks
abstract: With the ever-increasing proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices and advent in quantum computing, the need for quantum-secure cryptographic protocols is becoming more and more critical. This paper introduces a transformative approach to Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), integrating Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) and adaptive entanglement protocols for securing, scaling, and rendering IoT communications resilient. The proposed architecture is scalable, hardware-efficient, and noise-resilient, enabling AI-assisted protocol optimization, dynamic qubit allocation, and QNN-based noise mitigation. Simulations with Qiskit and PennyLane produce a fidelity of 99.9% and achieve an average QBER of 0.015, representing a 32% reduction compared to the 0.022 QBER typically reported for Measurement-Device-Independent-QKD (MDI-QKD). The proposed QNN model classifies with an accuracy of 97.5%, significantly outperforming the VQNN’s 80.5%. A hierarchical quantum authentication scheme is also proposed to ensure multilayer security in heterogeneous IoT settings.

title: Towards Quantum Network Performance Metrics: Challenges and Demonstration
abstract: As quantum networks move toward practical deployment, standardized performance monitoring becomes essential. This article proposes a structured monitoring framework for quantum networks with performance metrics, including quality (e.g., entanglement fidelity, QBER, loss, dark count rate), throughput and latency (e.g., entanglement rate, waiting time), timing (e.g., coincidence window, production and coincidence jitter), and exogenous factors (e.g., temperature, humidity, vibrations). These measurements enable real-time observability, benchmarking, and control, supporting use cases such as fault diagnosis, adaptive timing, and entanglement routing. Additionally, we implement a non-invasive prototype environmental monitoring system integrated with the quantum network infrastructure at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, demonstrating practical feasibility of live data collection and alert generation. Furthermore, we discuss the challenges of real-time monitoring and the trade-offs between observability and system performance. This work establishes a foundation for developing advanced quantum network monitoring systems and lays the groundwork for future autonomous control and quantum software-defined networking.

title: Quantum Communication with Quantum Dots Beyond Telecom Wavelengths via Hollow-Core Fibers
abstract: Quantum dot single-photon sources are promising for quantum communication. Yet, the most advanced devices operate near 900 nm, where standard single-mode fibers experience significant losses. We address this by employing a hollow-core fiber engineered for low-loss transmission at quantum dot wavelengths, with measured loss of 0.65 dB/km and potentially as low as 0.12 dB/km near 934 nm. The fiber also supports strong classical signals at 1550 nm without adding Raman noise. Using this platform, we transmit all four BB84 polarization states from an InAs quantum dot over 340 m with 0.1% QBER, preserving single-photon purity and indistinguishability even in the presence of a strong classical signal. These results highlight how tailored transmission media enable quantum networks beyond the limits of standard telecom fibers.

title: Data for "Quantum Communication with Quantum Dots Beyond Telecom Wavelengths via Hollow-Core Fibers"

abstract: This repository contains the data supporting the results presented in the manuscript “Quantum Communication with Quantum Dots Beyond Telecom Wavelengths via Hollow-Core Fibers” (pre-print version at https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11889).Due to the large data volume and the requirement of hardware-specific acquisition software, raw time-tag files are not included.
