title: Quantum Semantic Communication
abstract: Quantum communication has reached a rate bottleneck, yet enhancing its throughput remains of profound significance. Here we propose a scheme termed quantum semantic communication-a novel paradigm that integrates semantic communication with quantum secure direct communication to realize highly efficient, task-oriented, and intrinsically secure information transmission. In quantum semantic communication, meaningful semantic content is directly encoded into quantum states, whereby the fundamental laws of quantum physics guarantee inherent eavesdropping-detection capability and information-theoretic security. By harnessing semantic compression and artificial intelligence-assisted encoding strategies, this approach surpasses the intrinsic rate constraints of conventional quantum secure direct communication. Simulation results show that quantum semantic communication can surpass the Wyner secure information bound compared with conventional quantum secure direct communication systems and demonstrate its potential to break through the linear distance bound of quantum communication. These findings pave the way for high-rate secure communication.

title: Enhancing Cloud Data Security against Quantum Threats Using E91 QRD and Lattice-Based Encryption
abstract: Quantum computing gained popularity, posing a challenge to it. Severe threat against classical cryptography schemes such as RSA. Particularly where it is required on a large-scale cloud deployment, and AES. Manage secret national data. An integrated system of E91 Quantum Key Distribution with lattice-based encryption is needed to protect cloud information in the Indian environment. This architecture was inspired by workloads whose secrecy and authenticity are extreme, such as healthcare records that are linked to the Aadhaar, UPI transactions, and the like. In this work, we would like to find out whether there is a scalable solution that happens after the quantum phase. Some of the tasks that are included in the methodology are probability analysis, monitoring, QBER assessment, simulated key creation using E91, and benchmarking. Comparison with standard models of the encryption/decryption speed, CPU-memory consumption, communication overhead, and key-generation frequency. The results demonstrate that BB84 produces keys with lower QBER and higher entropy, whereas hybrid encryption outperforms lattice-only systems with key throughputs of around 900 kbps and just minimal overhead. When it comes to quantum resistance, advanced privacy, and essential randomness, comparative radar research shows that hybrids are preferable. The results are in: the hybrid strategy provides a future-proof, realistic means to protect data stored in the cloud against quantum attackers, even if it does need some extra bandwidth and resources, which makes it a good fit for large-scale deployments in India.

title: Performance Analysis of MDI-QKD in Thermal-Loss and Phase Noise Channels
venue: IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE)
abstract: Measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD), enhances quantum cryptography by mitigating detector-side vulnerabilities. This study analyzes MDIQKD performance in thermal-loss and phase noise channels, modeled as depolarizing and dephasing channels to capture thermal and phase noise effects. Based on this channel framework, we derive analytical expressions for Bell state measurement probabilities, quantum bit error rates (QBER), and secret key rates (SKR) of MDI-QKD. Our simulations reveal that SKR decreases exponentially with transmission distance, with performance further degraded by increasing thermal noise and phase noise, particularly under high thermal noise conditions. These findings offer insights into enhancing MDI-QKD's noise resilience, supporting secure key generation in practical, noisy environments.

title: Near‐hashing‐bound Quantum Turbo Short‐block Codes
abstract: This chapter introduces a family of near-hashing-bound, multiple-rate quantum turbo codes (QTCs) that combine quantum short-block codes (QSBCs) with quantum unity-rate codes (QURCs). The framework is based on transforming classical short-block codes into their quantum counterparts, yielding high-rate, scalable encoders having a minimum distance of d = 2. By concatenating QSBCs as outer codes with QURCs as inner codes, the proposed QSBC-QURC schemes support low-complexity, high-rate quantum error correction while operating very close to the quantum hashing bound. They also outperform the best-known QIrCC-QURC design. Their extrinsic information transfer (EXIT) chart analysis and the associated Monte Carlo simulations characterize their convergence behavior and their quantum bit error ratio (QBER) performance. The achievable goodput is also quantified. Furthermore, the multi-rate QTC concept is introduced, showing how the coding rate can be adaptively switched based on prevalent depolarizing probability to maintain specific fidelity or QBER levels, thereby providing a flexible and efficient design for quantum communication systems.

title: Synergetic Architectures for AI-Driven Quantum Cryptographic Protocols and Secure Communication
venue: International Conference on Smart Structures and Systems (ICSSS)
abstract: The current security systems cannot be considered long term sustainable because there is a quantum rate of development of the computing which directly and immediately threatens the classical cryptograph systems. In this respect, the research paper will undertake efforts in giving the concept of an AI-led adaptive mechanism of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols that will be self-sufficient in guarding and overseeing quantum communication networks against countermeasures towards the constantly evolving threats. The model combines quantum resources management and real-time threat analysis and optimization of dynamic parameter into one flow. Quantum channel noises can be predictedively implemented on machine learning using reinforcement learning, continued intrusion and anomaly detection on neural networks, and independent optimization of the parameters of QKD in dynamical communication systems. Post-quantum cryptography PQC algorithm-based lattice, hash-based and multivariate cryptography are also provided in the system as a backup mechanism to provide the confidence of the hybrid communication environments with the future compatibility of the classical and quantum infrastructural systems. In other cases, the framework will enhance quantum- enhanced blockchain where the AI-enhanced verification enhances the integrity of the distributed registries and resilience in the interparty communication networks. The ethical considerations and the need to have light and interoperative standards are the other considerations since it needs to be able to deploy on a large scale. Instead of calculating the performance standards, the provided research involves the conceptual architecture diagram of the way the predictive AI models can be logically aligned with the natural security features of quantum mechanics to a new generation cryptographic ecosystem that will be able to fight the classical and the quantum adversaries simultaneously.

title: Round-the-clock QKD over a free-space-fiber channel with passive polarization-basis compensation
venue: Frontiers in Quantum Science and Technology
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) enables information-theoretically secure communication by exploiting the quantum properties of single photons. Real-world deployment of QKD, however, requires reliable operation under uncontrolled environmental conditions where background illumination, atmospheric loss, coupling fluctuations, and polarization drift can significantly degrade performance. In this work, we experimentally demonstrate entanglement-based free-space QKD over an atmospheric channel with a passive, low-bandwidth polarization-correction strategy that avoids high-bandwidth real-time polarization tracking during the QKD acquisition. Using a 50-m free-space optical link implementing the BBM92 protocol, we compensate polarization scrambling arising from fiber birefringence and reference-frame misalignment by optimizing Bob’s measurement bases through quantum state tomography. QKD performance is evaluated across three 24-h acquisition campaigns spanning daylight and nighttime conditions, where high background noise, atmospheric fluctuations, and polarization drift pose significant challenges for secure key generation. By combining spectral, temporal, and spatial filtering with optimized coincidence-window selection, threshold-compatible average QKD performance is maintained across these acquisition campaigns. The optimized daylight key rate and QBER are ( 6.39 ± 0.81 k H z , 8.05 ± 1.48 % ) , while nighttime operation yields ( 6.98 ± 0.81 k H z , 8.25 ± 0.85 % ) . Under representative operating conditions with 8.3 % QBER, we obtain a final secure key rate of 351 H z after reconciliation and privacy amplification. To assess loss tolerance, we further emulate attenuation equivalent to a 1 k m free-space link using controlled attenuation, demonstrating approximately 6 k H z raw key rate under 30 % additional link loss. This attenuation study reproduces the additional loss budget only and does not constitute a physical kilometer-scale free-space demonstration. These results demonstrate that tomography-assisted measurement-basis correction can enable stable free-space entanglement-based QKD without high-bandwidth polarization tracking during key acquisition, providing a basis for future studies of more dynamic terrestrial and satellite-relevant quantum communication links.

title: Automated Active-Visibility-Control Loop for Stabilized DPS-QKD Decoding Under Dynamic Wavelength Drift
abstract: Automated and instantaneous stabilizing control of the quantum key decoder is the mandatory procedure, which guarantees real-time and high-speed differential-phase-shift (DPS) quantum key distribution (QKD) at low erroneous rate, and ensures the delay-line interferometric (DLI) decoding of the weak-coherent-pulse quantum bit-stream at a qualified and constant visibility. As the QKD system often suffers from environmental temperature/acoustic/vibrational perturbations, employing in situ software-controlled active-feedback-loop circuits is the alternative solution, which automatically preserves the constant visibility of a DLI decoder by dynamically tuning the wavelength of the weak-coherent-pulse carrier. To compensate for wavelength or phase inaccuracy, this work proposes the active-visibility-control (AVC) of the DLI by in situ monitoring its interferometric visibility and fine controls it with combined proportion-integral-loop and hill-climbing-stepper (PI-loop and HC-stepper) feedback algorithms, thus providing the 40-km-long SMF transmission of the weak-coherent-pulse bit-stream at 192-Mbit/s clock rate and 1-Mbit/s receiving rate. By adopting the PI-loop+HC-stepper combined algorithm to stabilize the long-term visibility of the AVC-DLI, such an AVC-DLI loop effectively overcomes environmental disturbances to confine the overall spectral linewidth and wavelength drift of the DPSQKD carrier within 266 kHz, and enabling the predicted lowest quantum bit-error-ratio (QBER) of 0.4% when decoding the weak-coherent-pulse bit at the first second. With the AVC-DLI, the back-to-back weak-coherent-pulse transmission guarantees a secure key rate of 91.6 kbit/s with a QBER stabilized to 1.8% over 10 min, and the long-reach capability is extended to 40-km transmission with a secure key rate of 2.6 kbit/s and QBER of 3.7% for 25–60 min. The technical improvement of AVC-DLI unveils the dynamic long-distance weak-coherent-pulse DPS-QKD transmission.

title: Spatially Adaptive Detection for Satellite-based QKD under Atmospheric Turbulence Channel
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) provides information-theoretic security and satellite-based quantum key distribution (SatQKD) has demonstrated the potential to extend this communication security to intercontinental scales. However, atmospheric turbulence induces significant distortion in the spatial distribution of received optical beams, while background noise remains approximately uniform across the detector plane. As a result, single-element qubit (quantum bit) detection can be frequently dominated by noise due to the random spatial pattern of the imaged wavefront, thereby degrading the system performance. To address this limitation, we propose to exploit the spatial degrees of freedom of single-photon detector arrays to reject the excessive noise while adapting to channel variations induced by turbulence. We develop a threshold-based selection method that only activates detector elements that have higher probability of registering qubits. We evaluate the performance of the proposed noise-rejection QKD schemes using Monte Carlo simulations considering the impact of diffraction and atmospheric turbulence on the transmitted optical beam in the presence of background and dark noise. The results show that, compared to conventional schemes, the proposed noise-rejection strategy effectively reduces the quantum bit error rate (QBER) and improves the secret key rate (SKR) performance, while the performance gains depend on the turbulence condition. These findings demonstrate the potential of adaptive array receiver design to enhance the robustness of the SatQKD system under realistic atmospheric conditions.

title: Asynchronous-bit-rate differential phase-shift-keying
abstract: An adaptive differential-phase-shifting (DPS) quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol improved by encoding asynchronous-bit-rate with harmonic clock tunability, decoded by shortened delay-line interferometer (DLI) with enhancing stability, and received by single-photon detection with long hold-off is demonstrated to realize low-erroneous transmission. To achieve long-term stabilized visibility with a maintained quantum bit-error-ratio (QBER) and secure key rate, the shortened and polarized DLI enlarges its free-spectral range (FSR) and reduces its power-to-wavelength slope (δP/δλ) to suppress its sensitivity to thermal gradient, channel leakage, and wavelength disturbance. Extremely low power and wavelength drifts of ΔP/P < ±0.02% and Δλ/λ = ±6.45 × 10−8 can be achieved, even when using a single-mode QKD carrier with a relatively broadened 300-kHz linewidth. Flexibly expanding the 1-bit-delay FSR of the polarized DLI from 0.04 to 1.00 GHz improves its immunity to environmental disturbances, enabling the DPS-QKD decoding with 210–213 patterns, 3.2% QBER, and 17.46-kbit/s under 0.22 photon/pulse in average. The asynchronous-bit-rate DPS-QKD protocol enables harmonic expansion of DLI’s FSR at limited single-photon avalanche detector’s bit rate, which lengthens the duration of stable visibility to support long-pattern DPS-QKD.

title: Democratizing Satellite Cybersecurity: A Hardware-Free, Multi-Layer Simulation Framework for Secure Space-to- Ground Non-Terrestrial Networks
venue: Indian Journal of Computer Science and Technology
abstract: Making sure communications stay safe in Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTNs) has become harder, mainly because cyber-physical attacks keep getting more advanced. Usual hardware-in-the-loop validation, it often complicates the testing process because it’s pricey, not very adaptable, and scalability constraints. To deal with that, we present the Smart Satellite Communication System (SSCS). This system is a wholly software-based, hardware-free simulation platform, designed to assess space-to-ground link resilience under complex, multi-layer threats. At the physical layer, the approach pairs an SGP4 orbital propagator using dynamic tracking loops to monitor Low Earth Orbit (LEO) passes and constantly adjusting for ±100 kHz changes in Doppler frequency.. For threat recognition, an unsupervised isolation forest model uses rolling amplitude variance features, converting that into intelligence for detecting organized electronic warfare jamming. Overall results show an AUC of 0.991. The model's accuracy is 91%. It also whitelists 697 out of 700 baseline communication frames, accomplishing that cleanly with no earlier threat signatures. On the cryptographic side, the simulation runs a BB84 Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocol, linking free-space optical photon loss to the Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) directly. When intercept-resend wiretapping is active, the observed QBER settles around 25% to 28% , which in practice is like performing a cryptographic cache purge at a 15% threshold. By monitoring both of these variable’s side by side, the system effectively separates the harmless weather-like rain fade (when QBER<10%) from the more questionable listening in behavior (QBER >20%) that is suspicious.Finally, SSCS runs on an async FastAPI ASGI arrangement, with full duplex WebSockets, so the end-to-end processing latency stays under 3 ms, even while the stress tests are handling about 5,000 packets per second.

title: Secure Simulation of BB84 and E91 Quantum Cryptography Protocols
abstract: Quantum computing is advancing rapidly and thus is a major challenge to traditional schemes of cryptographies like RSA, and ECC that get their security on computational difficulty. In order to counter this challenge, a paradigm change to be proposed is quantum cryptography which is based on the application of the rules of quantum mechanics to a conditional security. In the paper, a design and implementation of an interactive simulation platform, which models two seminal quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols, namely, BB84 and E91, is proposed. Formulated with a modular architecture in Streamlit, the system allows users to simulate the transmission into qubit, visualize key pre-processing, study the quantum bit error rate (QBER) and detect any eavesdropping through CHSH inequality. The platform will be used to include functionality of real-time graphical dashboards, user authentication, and a comparative analysis segment to systematically review classical and quantum-related cryptographic methods. The effects of noise levels, adversarial interference on the QBER and key generation rates are verified, and this serves to confirm the resilience of quantum systems against eavesdropping. The tool can be used as an educational and a research tool since it offers an intuitive interface to learn the quantum concepts related to superposition or entanglement and simultaneously takes the user through the protocol functionality in different security regimes. The findings attest to the increased security capabilities of quantum cryptographic systems, thus making them a valid option in the future communication network during the post-quantum era.

title: Quantum-Assisted Secure Nano-Network Traffic Framework for Real-Time Medical Data Transmission in Smart Hospitals
abstract: The integration of nano-sensor networks in smart hospitals enables high-resolution real-time monitoring of critical patient health metrics. However, the transmission of medical data over nano-networks poses significant challenges related to data security and anomaly detection. In this paper, we propose a deep learning (DL)-based anomaly classification framework integrated with quantum-assisted E91 protocol for secure key exchange. The framework classifies nano-traffic as normal or anomalous using lightweight models like TinyML, LSTM, and GRU, optimized via various optimizers. The E91 quantum key distribution (QKD) ensures secure and tamper-resistant transmission of classified medical data across hospital networks.

title: Broadband Polarization Compensation with Link Segment Reconstruction for Quantum Optical Links
abstract: Polarization-encoded quantum communication requires compensation of polarization transformations induced by the optical links. If the compensator is embedded between two channel segments, the transformations before and after the compensator must be treated separately. Moreover, standard three-wave-plate polarization controllers can become non-universal when their retardances deviate from their ideal values. To address these two challenges, we introduce a four-wave plate compensator that synthesizes arbitrary SO(3) polarization transformations over a broad wavelength range, and an eight-Stokes vector protocol that reconstructs the two link-segment Mueller matrices on either side of the compensator. Our experiment reveals that the four-plate sequence suppresses polarization-induced excess quantum bit error rate (QBER) to the sub-percent level at an operating wavelength more than 100 nm from the design wavelength without further optimization. Combined with two auxiliary wavelengths, our scheme tracks the temperature-driven drift of a strongly wavelength-sensitive fiber spool while keeping the excess QBER below 1%. These results support flexible compensator placement and wavelength channel selection, as well as non-interruptive polarization control in wavelength-division-multiplexed quantum optical links.

title: A Zero-Native-Dependency Post-Quantum Cryptographic Toolkit for Node.js: HPKE, LSH-256, and BB84 QKD
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Post-quantum cryptographic libraries for JavaScript/Node.js typically rely on native C/C addons or WebAssembly modules, introducing supply-chain risk and cross-platform compilation challenges. We present a zero-native-dependency post-quantum cryptographic toolkit implemented entirely using Node.js built-in crypto primitives (OpenSSL-backed). The toolkit includes: (1) a complete HPKE implementation (RFC 9180) supporting Base, PSK, Auth, and AuthPSK modes with DHKEM(X25519), HKDF-SHA256, and AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305; (2) LSH-256-256 (KS X 3262), a Korean standard hash function with 128-bit post-quantum collision resistance; and (3) a BB84 quantum key distribution simulation with basis reconciliation, eavesdrop detection, and privacy amplification. We describe the implementation approach, verify correctness against reference test vectors, and discuss the design principle of maximizing quantum resistance while minimizing dependency surface.

title: Characterisation of an InP-based PIC Transmitter in a QKD setup
venue: International Conference on Transparent Optical Networks
abstract: In this work, an indium phosphide (InP) based quantum key distribution (QKD) transmitter on a photonic integrated circuit (PICs) is examined. The PIC, which was designed by the authors from Eindhoven University of Technology, and characterised in the QKD system by the authors from Austrian Institute of Technology, features a ring laser structure, a single Mach-Zehnder modulator (MZM) structure with integrated radio frequency (RF) phase modulators for pulse carving, intensity modulation and phase modulation and an absorber for attenuation. The individual components were characterised. Additionally, the PIC was tested in a 4-state time-bin BB84 protocol including a bulk receiver, key performance measures like quantum bit error rate (QBER) and secret key rate (SKR) were analysed. The high performance PIC is capable of generating a SKR in the kbits/s range exhibiting high stability over a measured time frame of around an hour.

title: Finite key analysis of experimentally realized practical COW-QKD protocol
venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America B
abstract: An experimental implementation of the Coherent One-Way Quantum Key Distribution (COW-QKD) protocol is reported under realistic conditions, and a clean and easy-to-use framework for performing finite key analysis of the COW-QKD protocol is provided by extending a set of existing results. The framework provided here is used to perform finite key rate analysis of the COW-QKD protocol with respect to the actual parameters used in the experimental realization reported here. The system is kept running for several hours with different experimental parameters and stable secure key rates between 1.2 to 1.6 kbps are observed. In addition, QBER, phase error rate and secure key rate are obtained under finite key analysis, and it is shown that COW-QKD is secure for medium-range transmissions (up-to ~ 156 (171) km of optical fiber with 0.2 dB loss per km if detector efficiency is 0.1 (0.2) and other parameters are same as those used in this experiment).

title: Multimode fiber influence on single-photon avalanche diode timing jitter
abstract: The timing jitter of a single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) can be a limiting factor for the performance of quantum key distribution (QKD). Within QKD receiver modules, single mode fiber coupling has been extensively studied due to optical fiber-based demonstrations. However, multimode fiber, which is utilized for free-space demonstrations because it reduces the coupling losses, has been less extensively studied, but it is understood that multimode fibers will increase the timing jitter and decrease the performance of the detector as the fiber core diameter increases. Here, we present a collection of experimental analysis over the relationships between characteristics of multimode fiber such as length, core diameter and incident spot size and how this impacts the timing jitter of the detector. Additionally, we present analysis on the use of graded-index multimode fibers, mitigating for a portion of the impact on quantum bit error rate (QBER) due to multimode characteristics which can improve implementation of these receiver systems.

title: Quantum-Driven Intelligent Transportation Security
abstract: As cities deploy connected vehicles and data-intensive traffic platforms, intelligent transportation systems (ITS) face growing cyber–physical threats to data integrity, communication reliability, and user privacy. This chapter proposes the Quantum-Enhanced Mobility Security Framework (QEMSF), integrating quantum deep learning, blockchain-based trust mechanisms, and quantum key distribution (QKD) to secure Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication. Hybrid quantum–classical neural networks enable real-time anomaly detection, while decentralized ledgers and edge security support resilient, low-latency decisions. Case insights from Delhi, Singapore, and Seoul illustrate how QEMSF mitigates sensor spoofing, ransomware, and data interception, concluding with policy directions to strengthen trust and accountability in quantum-secured urban mobility systems.

title: UAV-Deployed OAM-BB84 QKD: Turbulence- and Misalignment-Resilient Decoy-State Finite-Key Security with AI-Assisted Calibration
abstract: We present a theoretical framework for quantum key distribution (QKD) using orbital angular momentum (OAM) encoded BB84 on an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) platform. A unified channel model captures Kolmogorov turbulence, pointing induced misalignment, and finite aperture clipping, enabling quantitative predictions of inter mode crosstalk and the resulting quantum bit error rate (QBER). Using a weak plus vacuum decoy state formulation, we derive composable finite key lower bounds on the secret key rate that incorporate statistical fluctuations, detector dark counts, efficiency mismatch, and error correction leakage. To stabilize performance under non stationary flight conditions, we introduce a lightweight physics informed learning module that combines physical priors with measured link statistics to classify valid pulses, reject corrupted data, and recommend decoding strategies. We outline a complete evaluation pipeline including UAV system architecture, turbulence driven QBER maps, decoy optimization, finite key scaling, and AI calibration metrics. Simulations indicate that under moderate turbulence and milliradian level pointing jitter, the proposed AI assisted method can improve the secret key rate by 10 percent to 30 percent while preserving composable security.

title: 6G quantum-classical signal convergence communication architecture with coordinated key management
abstract: With 5G networks enabling high-speed, low-latency communication, future 6G and quantum communications will require even higher data rates and enhanced security. Integrating quantum-safe technologies with classical systems through cofiber transmission enables the reuse of existing fiber infrastructure via multiplexing—reducing deployment costs and avoiding redundant construction. This approach offers a sustainable and environmentally friendly pathway for network evolution, positioning it as a key breakthrough in the development of secure 6G architecture.By leveraging Dense Wavelength Division Multiplexing (DWDM) over Optical Transport Networks (OTN), the system establishes an efficient bidirectional coordination framework between quantum and classical channels. The architecture incorporates multi-stage amplification, dispersion compensation, and an advanced optical-domain processing mechanism based on a "split-amplifycombine" scheme for quantum pulses. These features preserve signal integrity for both quantum and classical data while mitigating nonlinear effects. Additionally, the design includes a dual-mode key management system that meets the stringent requirements of 6G for high-speed responsiveness and large-scale concurrent quantum key distribution (QKD) through the dynamic coordination of real-time key generation and pre-stored keys. Crucially, the study analyzes Raman scattering noise in co-fiber transmission and reveals the distinct impacts of forward and backward Raman scattering on communication performance. Simulation results demonstrate that backward Raman scattering causes significantly greater degradation in secure key rate (SKR) and quantum bit error rate (QBER) than forward Raman scattering as transmission distance increases. Notably, forward Raman scattering yields better quantum communication performance metrics under ultra-long-distance transmission conditions.

title: The security of practical post-selection in Gaussian-modulated continuous-variable quantum key distribution
abstract: Abstract Gaussian-modulated coherent-state (GMCS) continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) offers a practical path to quantum-secured communication owing to its compatibility with existing optical fibre networks and use of mature security proofs. Achieving high secret key rates in real-time systems, however, requires post-processing schemes that are both information-theoretically efficient and computationally scalable. In previous experimental work 1 , we have demonstrated record real-time key rates using a one-round sliced reconciliation scheme with guard-band post-selection. Here, we present the corresponding theoretical framework and provide an asymptotic security analysis that considers arbitrary collective attacks, a much broader class of attacks than the usually assumed Gaussian collective attacks. The security analysis applies the entropic continuity of quantum channels justified by a quantum channel estimation procedure. In conditions of high noise, our scheme uses 500 times less classical communication than multidimensional reconciliation.

title: Trusted Online Key Management Center Architecture and Implementation Method for Train Control Systems
venue: IEEE International Conference on Trust, Security and Privacy in Computing and Communications (TrustCom)
abstract: Train control systems are critical for ensuring railway operational safety. With the advancement of railway intelligentization strategies and the rapid development of information technology, the train control system is evolving from closed to open systems. In this context, the security of the key management system(KMS) has become a core research direction, as the train-ground communication faces the risk of unauthorized access due to the use of open channels. Currently deployed KMS in industrial settings predominantly adopt offline architectures, which exhibit vulnerabilities to physical tampering during key storage and computation processes. Meanwhile, there is a general lack of research on the adaptation of mainstream online key management technologies (such as Hardware Security Modules (HSM), quantum key distribution(QKD), and Trusted Computing(TC)) in the context of rail train control systems. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an enhanced scheme based on an online key management mechanism. By integrating TC technology and optimizing the key distribution strategy, the scheme provides high-security protection throughout the full key lifecycle (generation, distribution, storage, and destruction). Experimental results demonstrate that, compared to traditional offline systems, the proposed solution significantly improves overall system security, resilience against attacks, and key update efficiency, thereby establishing a robust foundation for constructing highly secure modern railway train control systems.

title: Quantum Sensor Networks Security in the Information Era
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The convergence of information technology and quantum technology is ushering in the era of information physics, presenting unprecedented opportunities and challenges. Quantum sensors, leveraging quantum mechanical principles, are poised to revolutionize various fields, including environmental monitoring, navigation, and medical diagnostics. However, the deployment of quantum sensor networks introduces new security vulnerabilities due to the inherently sensitive nature of quantum states and the potential for eavesdropping and manipulation. This paper addresses the critical security challenges associated with quantum sensor networks within the information physics paradigm. We propose a novel security framework based on Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) and Quantum State Preservation (QSP) techniques. This framework aims to establish a robust and secure data transmission and storage system for quantum sensor networks, mitigating threats related to key compromise and state leakage. The core claim of this work is to provide a comprehensive security mechanism for quantum sensor networks. The proposed mechanism combines QKD and QSP to build a data transmission and storage scheme that protects the integrity and confidentiality of quantum sensor data. This paper outlines the key components of the framework, analyzes its security properties, and highlights its potential impact on the future of quantum sensor network deployments. ---

title: A Conceptual Hybrid Framework for Post-Quantum Security: Integrating BB84 QKD, AES, and Bio-inspired Mechanisms
abstract: Quantum computing is a significant risk to classical cryptographic, especially RSA, which depends on the difficulty of factoring large numbers. Classical factorization methods, such as Trial Division and Pollard's Rho, are inefficient for large keys, while Shor's quantum algorithm can break RSA efficiently in polynomial time. This research studies RSA's vulnerabilities under both classical and quantum attacks and designs a hybrid security framework to ensure data protection in the post-quantum era. The conceptual framework combines AES encryption for classical security, BB84 Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) for secure key exchange with eavesdropping detection, quantum state comparison for lightweight authentication, and a bio-inspired immune system for adaptive threat detection. RSA is vulnerable to Shor's algorithm, BB84 achieves full key agreement in ideal conditions, and it detects eavesdropping with high accuracy. The conceptual model includes both classical and quantum security methods, providing a scalable and adaptive solution for Post-Quantum encryption data protection. This work primarily proposes a conceptual framework. Detailed implementation, security proofs, and extensive experimental validation are considered future work.

title: Design & Development of a Quantum Antenna for Advanced Communication and Sensing Applications
venue: International Journal of Engineering & Extended Technologies Research
abstract: With the emergence of sixth-generation (6G) wireless networks, ensuring information-theoretic security at extremely high data rates has become a critical challenge. Conventional cryptographic techniques are increasingly vulnerable to quantum computing attacks, motivating the integration of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) with advanced wireless technologies. This paper proposes a hybrid QKD–Massive MIMO framework operating in the terahertz (THz) band (10–30 THz) to evaluate secure key generation performance under realistic distance, frequency, and antenna scaling conditions. A security-aware Secret Key Rate (SKR) model is developed by incorporating Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) constraints and distance-dependent attenuation. Extensive simulations analyze SKR variation with transmission distance (1–10 m), carrier frequency, and antenna array size (32–1024). Results demonstrate that massive MIMO significantly enhances SKR and extends the secure communication range, while higher THz frequencies introduce stronger attenuation. The proposed framework validates the feasibility of scalable quantum-secure THz communications for future 6G networks.

title: Finite-Key Analysis of BB84 and B92 QKD with Discrete Phase Randomization and Koashi Bound
abstract: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) enables theoretically secure key exchange based on fundamental quantum principles such as the no-cloning theorem and Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle. However, practical implementations remain vulnerable to side-channel attacks caused by device imperfections, while many existing studies primarily analyze asymptotic security or isolated attack scenarios rather than realistic finite-key conditions. Unlike prior studies that focus on asymptotic or single-attack analyses, this work presents a comprehensive finite-key security evaluation of BB84 and B92 protocols under hybrid side-channel attacks using Discrete Phase Randomization (DPR) as a lightweight mitigation strategy and the Koashi bound for improved phase-error estimation in B92. Numerical simulations are performed using realistic system parameters with a finite-key size of 100 billion pulses across ten representative attack scenarios. The results show that applying DPR (M = 32) significantly suppresses phase-sensitive attack-induced errors, reducing the quantum bit error rate (QBER) from 11–50% to approximately 1.5–3.02%, thereby restoring practical secure key generation. B92 with the Koashi bound achieves secure transmission distance improvements from 181.6 km to 190.8 km without attacks and reaches 187.0 km under hybrid attacks with DPR, slightly exceeding BB84 in certain conditions. Peak secret key rates reach 0.1363 bit/pulse for BB84 and 0.0741 bit/pulse for B92. These findings demonstrate that non-orthogonal protocols can remain competitive under realistic finite-key constraints using practical mitigation techniques, although literature based induced QBER assumptions remain a limitation.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Information Encoding and Decoding
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel information encoding and decoding scheme leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. The core concept involves utilizing multi-particle entangled states for superposition-based encoding and subsequent information recovery through measurement outcomes. Furthermore, the scheme incorporates entanglement-assisted eavesdropping detection and error correction mechanisms. The theoretical analysis demonstrates the potential to surpass the classical channel capacity limit, fundamentally altering the landscape of information transmission. The proposed approach explores the physical boundaries of information transfer, offering a new pathway for quantum communication protocols. The key mathematical elements underpinning the system are presented, including the quantum state description, measurement operators, and the relevant equations governing the process. The system's performance is evaluated through theoretical modeling, highlighting its advantages in terms of information rate and security.

title: Enhancement of IoT Device through Post Quantum Cryptographic Protocols and Lamport–Diffie One-Time Signature Scheme
abstract: The rapid growth of the IoT has led to more cyberattacks on low-power devices. This study presents the IPQCLD model, which uses advanced security measures for future IoT networks to address these issues. It applies data preprocessing methods like Min-Max normalization and LDA, quantum key distribution using the BB84 protocol, and post-quantum cryptography techniques such as Lamport-Diffie one-time signatures. These features enhance authentication, encryption, and attack detection. The Lamport-Diffie method blocks key reuse and authenticates messages, while the BB84 protocol helps detect eavesdropping for secure key exchange. LDA and Min-Max normalization simplify data management and ensure accurate detection. Simulation results show that IPQCLD significantly outperforms baseline models, achieving a precision of 0.95 and a recall rate of 0.90.

title: Quantum Guard: Adaptive Device-Independent QKD and Practical File Encryption Using Real Quantum Hardware Key
venue: International Conference on Knowledge Engineering and Communication Systems (ICKECS)
abstract: The rapid advancement of quantum computing threatens to undercut the mathematical foundations of today’s public-key cryptosystems. Quantum key distribution (QKD) provides an information-theoretically secure substitute whose security is derived from physical laws rather than computational complexity. However, most practical QKD systems still rely on trusted hardware components that are vulnerable to manufacturing backdoors, misalignment, and side-channel leakage. Device-Independent Quantum Key Distribution (DIQKD) removes these assumptions by certifying security from experimentally observed Bell-inequality violations, treating devices as untrusted black boxes.This paper provides a complete overview of DIQKD research, focusing on the evolution from early theoretical security proofs to real-world demonstrations on quantum hardware. We review implementation issues on platforms like IBM Quantum, evaluate finite-key security models, and study fundamental protocols. Building on this review, the Quantum Guard framework is presented as a conceptual design that combines adaptive optimization, finite-key estimation, and active attack detection to achieve resilient, device-independent communication. We further demonstrate practical file encryption using DIQKD-generated keys. Finally, we discuss current limitations and strategic objectives for building scalable, commercial quantum-secure networks.

title: Polarization correction towards satellite-based QKD without an active feedback
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is a cryptographic protocol to enable two parties to share a secure key string, which can be used in one-time pad cryptosystem. There has been an ongoing surge of interest in implementing long-haul photonic-implementation of QKD protocols. However, the endeavour is challenging in many aspects. In particular, one of the major challenges is the polarization degree of freedom of single-photons getting affected while transmission through optical fibres, or atmospheric turbulence. Conventionally, an active feedback-based mechanism is employed to achieve real-time polarization tracking. In this work, we propose an alternative approach where we first perform a state tomography to reconstruct the output density matrix. We then evaluate the optimal measurement bases at Bob's end that leads to the maximum (anti-)correlation in the measurement outcomes of both parties. As a proof-of-principle demonstration, we implement an in-lab BBM92 protocol -- a particular variant of a QKD protocol using quantum entanglement as a resource -- to exemplify the performance of our technique. We experimentally generate polarization-entangled photon pairs having $94\%$ fidelity with $\ketψ_1 = 1/\sqrt{2}\,(\ket{HV}+\ket{VH})$ state and a concurrence of $0.92$. By considering a representative 1 ns coincidence window span, we are able to achieve a quantum-bit-error-rate (QBER) of $\approx 5\%$, and a key rate of $\approx 35$ Kbps. The protocol performance is independent of local polarization rotations through optical fibres. We also develop an algorithmic approach to optimize the trade-off between the key rate and QBER. Our approach obviates the need for active polarization tracking. Our method is also applicable to entanglement-based QKD demonstrations using partially mixed as well as non-maximally entangled states, and extends to single-photon implementations over fibre channels.

title: Quantum-Resilient Cryptography and Safe Guarding Post Quantum Cryptographic Protocols Against Quantum Threats
venue: International Conference on Pervasive Computing and Social Networking (ICPCSN)
abstract: The Hybrid approach in Quantum Cryptography creates adaptable security model which provides the safest Communication in the emerging quantum era. The development of quantum computing raise questions about the long-term security. Traditional algorithms, such as RSA, ECC, and Diffie-Hellman, which is seemed computationally secure but it can be effectively solved by quantum algorithms such as Shor's and Grover's. This problem leads to the origination of two key trends in current studies, namely Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC), designing mathematical approaches to encryption resistant to quantum attacks; Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) using the principles of quantum mechanics to assure security in communications. Accordingly, this research proposes a hybrid security framework including reliable data encryption and authentication using PQC, combined with the safe key- exchange method of QKD. The model is implemented in Python, Qiskit, and PQClean's Kyber and Dilithium algorithms to show how these two paradigms can cooperate toward quantum- resilient communication. To present the system performance, key exchange efficiency, computational overhead, and security strength have been considered. According to the results, this hybrid approach gives superior defense against quantum threats while maintaining practical effectiveness for real-world applications such as cloud security, 6G networks, and the Internet of Things.

title: Transformasi Keamanan Maritim Adaptif Melalui Inovasi Teknologi Kuantum Dalam Menghadapi Ancaman Hibrida Global
abstract: This research analyzes the paradigm shift in maritime security driven by two main trends: the escalation of hybrid threats and the maturity of quantum technology. The analysis reveals that modern hybrid threats exploit fundamental vulnerabilities, including ambiguity in detection, attribution, and law, which creates conditions of "sea blindness," as well as cybersecurity vulnerabilities in increasingly integrated digital and navigational infrastructure. The key finding of this study is that quantum technology offers symmetric and fundamental countermeasures to these vulnerabilities. Quantum sensors, including atom interferometerbased PNT, NV-center-based precision magnetometry, and Distributed Quantum Sensing (DQS) networks, provide high transparency and precise measurement. This directly diminishes ambiguities, addresses "sea blindness," and alters the strategic calculus of hybrid actors by eliminating plausible deniability. Additionally, quantum communication, particularly Underwater QKD (UQKD), offers absolute security for critical data links, enhancing the resilience of Critical Maritime Infrastructure (CMI) and sensor architecture against cyber interception and manipulation. The synthesis of precision sensors, secure communication, and AI-based data fusion forms the foundation for a new "adaptive maritime security architecture." This architecture is proactive, resilient, and capable of operating independently of vulnerable external infrastructure.

title: Unconditionally Secure Control and Diagnostic Systems
venue: Proceedings of the Annual Conference of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society
abstract: This paper presents an information-theoretically (unconditionally) secure approach to enhancing security of control and diagnostic applications. Unconditional (information-theoretic) security means that an attacker, even with infinite computational power, still cannot decrypt the data. Currently, only quantum key distribution (QKD) and the Kirchhoff-law-Johnson-noise (KLJN) schemes can offer unconditional security for the secure key generation/exchange, which is the difficult part to reach information-theoretic security. The key idea of this paper is to deploy the chip-integrable and equally (or more) secure KLJN approach to enhancing the security of control and diagnostic systems. We will present the high level architecture and three potential applications of our approach.

title: Phase stabilization of high-bandwidth squeezed and entangled states over 1km distributed optical fiber
abstract: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is a technology for secure communication between two parties, using the principles of quantum mechanics. Our continuous-variable QKD experiment implements a fiber-based scheme connecting two laboratories in two separated buildings (building A and B). We set up an Gaussian continuous-variable entanglement source in building A, consisting of two squeeze lasers to generate two-mode squeezed states. They are shared between the two buildings via a 1 km optical fiber. In both buildings, the entangled states are measured with self-designed and self-built balanced homodyne detectors. Due to the entanglement, the results are quantum random (truly random) but also correlated and can be used to generate a secret key. Attacks on the channel as well as on devices in building B reduce the entanglement strength and can thus be quantified. A major challenge in this setup is the phase stabilization and measurement synchronization between the two buildings. The fibers pick up extra noise, such as seismic and acoustic and experience temperature drifts. In this work, I will introduce the experiment, discuss the problem of phase noise and our approach to a control scheme. The first results with squeezed (not entangled) states show promising results for a phase lock of entangled states.

title: A Quantum AI-Enabled Framework for Secure Image Watermarking in Cryptographic and Cybersecurity Applications
abstract: Protecting the ownership of pictures and the integrity of copyright law is now of paramount importance with the explosion in digital content, especially content that is vulnerable to manipulation and distribution without the copyright owner's permission. This research work combines post-quantum cryptography, Artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum computing aspects to introduce ground breaking quantum intelligent and secure architecture for image watermarking. The proposed system is using quantum transform methods for inserting undetectable and tamper- proof quantum watermarks into digital images. AI models are then applied to the images for change detection and immediate verification of the authenticity of the watermark. Therefore, quantum key distribution (QKD), lattice-based post-quantum cryptography and other quantum safe encryption schemes are employed to cryptographically secure the metadata of watermark for good cryptographic security. This hybrid approach has been shown to enhance the security against both classical and quantum attacks. NFT authentication, secure cloud storage of pictures, and protection for copyright in digital media are examples of some potential applications. Simulation and experimental results show increased strength of the watermark, accuracy of message about unauthorized insertion of the watermark, and enhanced cryptographic security with respect to all other methods. The article demonstrates how AI can be aligned with quantum computing in order to secure audio-visual content in post-quantum cyber security.

title: Feasibility of entanglement-based QKD protocols with SPDC and quantum-dot sources.
abstract: We theoretically analyze the feasibility of entanglement-based quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols-both device-independent QKD (DI-QKD) and entanglement-based BB84 (EPR-BB84)-using widely employed spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) and what we believe to be a novel semiconductor quantum-dot (QD) sources. Within a unified photodetection-theory framework, we jointly evaluate the Bell parameter, quantum bit error rate (QBER), and asymptotic Devetak-Winter secret key rate for both source types, accounting for multiphoton emission in SPDC, fine-structure splitting (FSS) in the QD, and imperfect detection including finite efficiency and dark counts. Our results demonstrate that, despite the detrimental effect of FSS, QD sources achieve sufficient Bell violation and positive secret key rates under realistic experimental conditions. In contrast, within the standard CHSH-based DI-QKD framework and the detection and binning strategies, bare SPDC sources do not yield a positive secret key rate, despite the feasibility of loophole-free Bell tests with such sources. Our findings are crucial for the practical implementation of entanglement-based QKD protocols using realistic sources and detectors.

title: FedQ-Fraud: A Quantum-Enforced Federated Learning Framework for Financial Fraud Detection
venue: ACM International Symposium on Theory, Algorithmic Foundations, and Protocol Design for Mobile Networks and Mobile Computing (MobiHoc)
abstract: The rapid growth of online financial transactions has made fraud detection a critical priority, especially with evolving fraud strategies that evade traditional systems. This paper presents a novel and secure fraud detection framework integrating Deep Learning (DL), Federated Learning (FL), and Quantum Encryption Communication (QEC). Our approach ensures high fraud detection accuracy while maintaining user data privacy and secure communication. We implemented a 3-layer GRU model using the MOON algorithm under the FL paradigm and achieved a global accuracy of 97.47%, outperforming traditional models like LSTM, 1D-CNN and XGBoost. To secure model parameter exchange between clients and server, we evaluated two entanglement-based Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols — BBM92 and MDI-QKD. Experimental results revealed BBM92 to be more stable and suitable for integration with FL, demonstrating superior average secret key rate (SKR) and lower quantum bit error rate (QBER). The proposed system effectively combines accuracy, privacy, and quantum security, making it a scalable solution for real-world fraud detection.

title: Ensuring Safety of Financial Institutions in the Modern Era Through Quantum Computing and Cybersecurity
venue: Advances in computational intelligence and robotics book series
abstract: Quantum computing imperils cybersecurity by utilizing superposition and entanglement—via algorithms like Grover's and Shor's—to breach classical RSA and ECC encryption. To secure critical economic data, particularly within European banks, the adoption of lattice-based, hash-based, and code-based cryptography, along with Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), is essential. This paper outlines a future “Architecture of Quantum Banking” (AQB) rooted in post-quantum cryptography. Beyond defense, the study explores how financial institutions can leverage QAOA and Quantum Monte Carlo simulations to optimize portfolios, accelerate derivative pricing, and enhance fraud detection. Additionally, quantum-enhanced machine learning and blockchain integration promise superior anomaly detection and transaction security. To navigate scaling challenges, the research emphasizes the necessity of collaboration between banks, technology firms, and research institutes to balance innovation with robust risk management.

title: Application of Quantum-AI Security in Intelligent Transportation
abstract: This chapter offers an overall architecture of Quantum-AI Security in ITS, with main emphasis on threat modeling, post-quantum cryptography, AI-based anomaly detection, and privacy-preserving data management. It discusses the ways hybrid classical quantum architectures can be used to optimize traffic in real-time, provide secure V2X communication, and achieve resilient infrastructure functionality. The chapter further looks at quantum key distribution, post-quantum secure routing, adversarial attack mitigation of AI model, and regulation to safeguard the privacy of users. Real world deployment issues, system architecture and interoperability with existing standards are also addressed to make sure that it will be scalable and trustworthy. The proposed security framework, based on the combination of quantum resilience and AI intelligence, will improve the safety, privacy, and reliability of transportation ecosystems, which will result in the creation of secure, autonomous, and sustainable mobility.

title: Cumulative Polarization Rotation Angle in Fiber-Optic Communication Lines Under Lightning Electromagnetic Impact
venue: Wave Electronics and its Application in Information and Telecommunication Systems (WECONF)
abstract: The problem of quantitative description of the total effect of electromagnetic fields of lightning discharges on the polarization state (SOP) of light in fiber-optic communication lines (FOCL) of the ITU-T G. 652 standard is considered. The cumulative angle parameter is proposed, which is defined as the integral of the norm of the local Stokes rotation vector along the line length, taking into account random birefringence, magnetooptical Faraday effect and electro-optical Kerr effect. Using the Jones matrix formalism, analytical expressions for cumulative polarization rotation angle are obtained in terms of the Verde constant, the induction of the lightning magnetic field, and the correlation length of the polarization-mode dispersion (PMD). It is established that the cumulative angle is related to the dynamic differential group delay (DGD), as well as to the quantum error coefficient QBER for the BB84 quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol. Based on the obtained dependences, a classification of exposure modes (I-IV) is formed according to the lightning current amplitude and the distance to the discharge channel. Numerical estimates are derived for SSMF (G. 652), DSF (G. 653), and NZ-DSF (G. 655) fibers with line lengths up to 50 km and lightning currents of$\mathbf{1 0 - 1 0 5 ~ k A}$. It is shown that at Category I currents (over 105 kA) at a distance of 100 m, the rate of SOP change reaches$17.5 \text{Mrad} / \mathrm{s}$, which leads to a critical increase in QBER and termination the QKD session. The results allow us to use the cumulative angle as a single integral criterion for lightning resistance of high-speed and quantum fiber-optic lines in the design of routes and justification of lightning protection parameters.

title: Security and Capacity Analysis of Vacuum State Jamming in Quantum Free Space Optical Communication
venue: IEEE International Conference on Advanced Networks and Telecommunications Systems
abstract: Free-space optical (FSO) quantum communication offers strong potential for secure, high capacity data transmission, but remains vulnerable to covert physical-layer attacks. This paper presents a rigorous analysis of vacuum state jamming—an adversarial strategy where the jammer probabilistically replaces transmitted pulses with vacuum states, thereby reducing effective photon counts without adding excess noise. We consider a binary phase-shift keying coherent-state quantum system over a Gamma–Gamma atmospheric turbulence channel. A consistent mixture model is developed for the jammed states, and optimal Helstrom detection is applied to derive exact expressions for the quantum bit error rate (QBER) under turbulence and jamming. For secure information throughput, the Holevo capacity is evaluated numerically from density operator eigenvalues. Numerical results confirm that vacuum jamming induces measurable degradation of both QBER and Holevo capacity, with stronger effects under high turbulence and lower signal energies. Comparisons between exact integral results and common approximations highlight the latter’s limited validity range. The framework not only quantifies the resilience of quantum FSO links against vacuum jamming, but also provides a foundation for developing jamming-aware monitoring and countermeasures.

title: Continuous-variable quantum secure direct communication with one-time pad
abstract: Abstract Quantum secure direct communication (QSDC) enables the direct transmission of secret messages over a quantum channel without prior key sharing. QSDC implemented in the continuous-variable (CV) regime allows high-capacity information transmission using simple optical communication technologies. In this work, we propose a novel CV-QSDC protocol with a quantum one-time pad, which achieves secure message transmission based on coherent states and unitary operations, and the receiver can directly obtain the secret messages after measuring the coherent states. The security of this protocol is jointly guaranteed by one-time pad encryption and a CV quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol. Performance analysis shows that the proposed scheme can achieve a quantum bit error rate (QBER) lower than 1% by adjusting the modulation variance and unitary operation parameters. With the optimal modulation variance, the secure transmission distance of the proposed protocol can exceed 150 km.

title: Quantum Leaps in the Sky: Composable XOR–Relay QKD over HAPs for Next-Gen 6G Networks
venue: IEEE World Forum on Internet of Things (WF-IoT)
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) via free-space optical (FSO) links suffers from severe turbulence losses and limited range in satellite-to-ground scenarios. We propose a two-hop XOR-relay architecture employing a high-altitude platform (HAP) to segment the link, reducing both geometric and atmospheric attenuation. Our simulation framework incorporates beam wandering, finite-key constraints, and realistic link geometry. Simulation results show up to a 55 times transmittance gain, 18% energy-per-bit savings, and a 64.2 kb/s secret key rate with under 3 ms latency. We formulate a constrained min–max optimization to minimize worst-case delay while meeting key rate, quantum bit error rate (QBER), and protocol overhead bounds. The XOR relay ensures composable secrecy with negligible information leakage, confirming the feasibility of stratospheric relays for low-latency, quantum-secure backhaul in future 6G non-terrestrial networks.

title: QKD-Enabled Optical Wireless Communication System for Ultra-Secure Defense Networks
abstract: The growing role of secure communication in defense networks has increased the need for systems that remain dependable even under advanced cyber-threat conditions. In this work, we study a Quantum Key Distribution (QKD)-enabled Optical Wireless Communication (OWC) link for short-range building-to-building applications. The system is evaluated using a MATLAB-based simulation framework that models a terrestrial free-space optical channel affected by attenuation, beam divergence, pointing misalignment, turbulence-related penalties, and additive noise. Accordingly, the performance of channel impairments is investigated with respect to QBER and the achievable secret key rate using the BB84 protocol. At the same time, a regression model based on ANN is developed to estimate the secret key rate from the measurable channel parameters. Finally, the derived key is used in the example of QOTP encryption to illustrate the secure end-to-end communication. It is concluded from the results that attenuation of channels has the most profound effect on the performance of QKD, particularly under high-loss situations where the key rate significantly decreases. In summary, the results provide a practical baseline for understanding QKD behavior over terrestrial FSO links and point to the need for future experimental verification.

title: Passive Pauli Toggling of Polarization Qubits in Optical Fibers: Error Bounds and QKD Performance
abstract: Polarization qubits offer a direct route to fiber-based quantum communication, yet the fiber that carries them also scrambles their reference frame through uncontrolled birefringence. Active compensation commonly relies on monitoring and feedback, raising a natural question: can the link itself suppress coherent polarization drift before it reaches the receiver? We show that it can within a regime of sufficiently correlated unitary drift. Our central idea is to embed a fixed cyclic sequence of Pauli rotations along the fiber, turning propagation distance into a spatial toggling frame. Rather than estimating and inverting the unknown transformation, the sequence repeatedly reverses its leading action. We establish exact refocusing for constant generators compatible with a two-segment echo, show that a four-frame Pauli cell cancels the leading contribution of any traceless quasi-static generator, and bound the residual error for smoothly varying birefringence. We then connect these guarantees to operational BB84 quantities, including measured QBERs, the resulting secret fraction, and insertion loss. In simulations of a 50 km fiber with spatially correlated birefringence, a representative design reduces the mean QBER from 6.11% to 0.224% at a device spacing of 1.25 km. With an assumed per-device transmission of t = 0.997, this raises the asymptotic key rate per launched pulse by a factor of approximately 2.5. For this parameter set, the best design in the tested scan is not the densest one: error suppression and optical loss create a finite operating window. These results provide a loss-aware design principle for passive polarization stabilization and suggest a low-overhead complement to active tracking in polarization-encoded QKD networks.

title: Harmonic Resonance in High-Dimensional Manifolds: A Unified Framework for Sub-Threshold Information Recovery, Quantum Encryption, and Deep Space Transception
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper introduces a novel computational and physical framework, designated "Frames of Decay," which rejects the static scalar architectures of traditional digital networks in favor of continuous dynamic trajectories across an angular Riemann hypersphere. We formalize the mathematical boundary conditions of attentional gate collapse and demonstrate that state transitions leave a lingering geometric residue on the underlying computational substrate ("residue on the glass"). To recover this sub-threshold data without the overhead of cryogenic cooling environments, we propose an ambient-temperature (293 K) solid-state hardware aperture utilizing synthetic diamond matrices embedded with Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers, thermally insulated by a custom photonic crystal metamaterial bandgap. The system tracks fading signal densities via a modified advection-diffusion-reaction equation, translating phase rotations into structured outputs through a discrete musical tuning matrix (4186.08 Hz → 2939.40 Hz). Finally, we validate this fractional geometric framework by aligning it with subatomic weak force anomalies (1.9% Z → N N-bar decay deviation) and macroscopic geodetic reference frames (Lense-Thirring relativistic frame dragging). Dual-use applications for deep space laser transception (Rx/Tx) and quantum key distribution (QKD) eavesdropping detection are detailed.

title: Quantum Frontiers
venue: Advances in computational intelligence and robotics book series
abstract: This chapter examines the intersection of quantum computing, cybersecurity, and adversarial machine learning (AML), outlining both transformative opportunities and emerging risks. Quantum computing, leveraging superposition and entanglement, offers unparalleled computational speed-ups but simultaneously threatens classical cryptographic protocols via Shor's and Grover's algorithms. Meanwhile, AML reveals vulnerabilities in machine learning systems through evasion, poisoning, and inference attacks, posing risks in healthcare, finance, and autonomous domains. Quantum power could accelerate adversarial exploits yet also enhance defenses through anomaly detection, quantum key distribution, and hybrid quantum–classical security models. Persistent challenges—error correction, scalability, cost, and integration—limit deployment. The chapter underscores the urgency of adopting post-quantum cryptography, fortifying AML defenses, and promoting collaboration between quantum scientists and cybersecurity experts, concluding with a roadmap for building resilient, quantum-secure infrastructures.

title: Secure Communication for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships Using Quantum-Satellite Relays
abstract: This paper introduces a secure federated learning (FL) system aimed at detecting anomalies in the communication of maritime autonomous surface ships (MASS). The model effectively distinguishes between normal and anomalous nano-traffic while safeguarding data privacy among distributed clients. To bolster security, Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols, such as BB84 and E91, are utilized for encrypted key exchange during ship-to-ship and ship-to-ground interactions. The suggested framework demonstrates consistent performance enhancement, achieving individual client accuracies of 0.77, 0.79, and 0.81, with the global model reaching an accuracy of 0.83. Moreover, the global model’s loss significantly reduces from 0.92 to 0.55 across five rounds, indicating successful convergence. These findings reinforce the framework’s efficacy in providing secure, decentralized anomaly detection within maritime networks. Future research will focus on incorporating neuromorphic architectures with FL to improve real-time performance in MASS communication.

title: Quantum-Secured AI-IoT Frameworks
venue: Advances in computational intelligence and robotics book series
abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) is transforming digital ecosystems, offering automation, predictive intelligence, and real-time decision-making. However, increasing interconnectivity raises serious concerns about data security, privacy, and trust. This chapter introduces the AI-IoT Security Integration Framework (AISIF), a multi-layered architecture combining AI-based analytics, blockchain-led trust management, and quantum-secure encryption to build resilient and privacy-preserving systems. The framework employs federated learning for secure data collaboration, Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) for encryption, and explainable AI for transparent decision-making. Through two case studies smart healthcare and smart grid systems the framework demonstrates improvements in anomaly detection accuracy, latency reduction, and intrusion response efficiency. The findings highlight that integrating AI intelligence with quantum security ensures sustainable, trustworthy, and adaptive IoT infrastructures for future intelligent environments.

title: Optimization of Secret Key Rate for BB84 under Collective Rotation Noise
abstract: Practical quantum key distribution (QKD) systems operate under noise, but security of most protocols have been analyzed under ideal noiseless scenarios. In this work, we investigated security performance of BB84 protocol under effect of collective rotation noise. Using theoretical quantum information frameworks, we analyzed key security parameters including quantum bit error rate (QBER), mutual information and secret key rate (SKR). Security of protocol is studied under various eavesdropping scenarios based on intercept and resend attacks. Our results show that collective rotation noise has a significant impact on the information shared between the two parties. Particularly, we extended prior treatments by suggesting a noise engineering strategy where we identified a non-zero noise range where information accessed by Eve is minimized while corresponding SKR degradation remains relatively small. This analysis provide insights into robustness of BB84 protocol under realistic noisy channels and may contribute towards development of more resilient QKD systems.

title: Quantum cryptography for secure messaging
venue: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews
abstract: The project “Quantum Cryptography for Secure Messaging” aims to create a highly secure communication system using the BB84 protocol, a key method in quantum key distribution. As traditional encryption systems face growing threats from cyberattacks and future quantum computers, this project provides a future-proof solution for message encryption. It uses simulated quantum bits (qubits) to generate secret keys based on quantum mechanics, ensuring that any eavesdropping attempts can be detected instantly. The process involves encoding binary data into quantum states, securely exchanging keys, and applying them for symmetric encryption of messages. Key features include real-time key generation, automatic encryption and decryption, and intrusion detection. The expected outcome is a working prototype of a secure messaging system that can resist both current and emerging security challenges, highlighting the potential of quantum cryptography as a foundation for the next generation of digital security.

title: A comparative analysis of InGaAs SPADs and SNSPDs in entanglement-based Quantum communications
venue: International Conference on Transparent Optical Networks
abstract: We present experimental results from a Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) setup based on entanglement, where polarization entangled photon pairs are distributed after narrowband filtering and followed by detection employing polarization-based receivers. A comparative analysis of the performance of InGaAs single photon avalanche detectors (SPADs) and superconducting nanowire single photon detectors (SNSPDs), reveals a notable advantage of SNSPDs for QKD applications. The entangled photon pairs are generated using a Sagnac-based polarization entanglement source, and subsequently split by Dense Wavelength Division Multiplexers (DWDMs). These entangled photon pairs are sent to two polarization-based receivers facilitating the comparison between the detection using InGaAs SPADs and SNSPDs. The results emphasize the superior performance of SNSPDs reflected in an around 80 times higher coincidence rate, therefore tolerating around 8 dB higher attenuation values. For both configurations and all considered attenuation levels, the fidelity and quantum bit error rate (QBER) are well inside the respective bounds for secure key generation. This work provides valuable insights for the optimization of QKD systems.

title: itu-kcomm: ITU Pass-2 Development Toolkit #14 (Communications Information Theory K_comm)
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Copyright (C) 2026 Munehiro Terada. Licensed under CC-BY-4.0. ITU Pass-2 Development Research artifact #14. Python toolkit implementing K_comm modular Hamiltonian on H_comm = H_source ⊗ H_channel ⊗ H_code ⊗ H_modulation ⊗ H_protocol, with four operational pillars: Shannon 1948: entropy H(X) = -Σ p_i log p_i, joint/mutual information, binary symmetric channel capacity C = 1 - H(p), and Shannon-Hartley AWGN capacity C = B log2(1 + SNR). Source coding: Huffman 1952 prefix code with average length L verified to satisfy H ≤ L < H + 1; Shannon-Fano-Elias code with explicit length ⌈log2(1/p)⌉ + 1. Cellular generations: 2G GSM (1991 Radiolinja FI) → 3G UMTS (2001.10 NTT DoCoMo FOMA) → 4G LTE (2009.12.14 TeliaSonera) → 5G NR (3GPP Rel-15 2018.6, KR 2019.4.3) → 6G IMT-2030 (ITU-R M.2160-0, 2023.6.22 decision, 2023.11 publication). 3GPP Rel-15 through Rel-20 schedule.
