encryption methods.By integrating quantum computing into e-commerce cybersecurity allows online companies to establish a proactive and robust approach for protecting customer data.

title: Decoy state-based time synchronization
abstract: Time synchronization is a crucial requirement in quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols, ensuring accurate key generation via the correct assignment of bits of raw key and enabling eavesdropping detection via the precise recording of photon statistics. State-of-the-art experiments typically use an extra channel to synchronize the clocks of the transmitter and receiver via classical signals. In this work, we study the possibility of performing clock synchronization via the signals used for the key generation, which are already present in decoy-state-based BB84 protocols. Without altering the protocol in any way, we use the different mean photon numbers of the signal and decoy states for time synchronization without a dedicated physical channel capable of clock synchronization. The proposed method relies only on the photons sent and received for key generation and does not require any change to the QKD protocol. The only change in the experiment is on the software level, thus making it very simple to implement. We demonstrate a clock synchronization method in a simulation of a specific fiber-based QKD experiment. Like other decoy-state-based BB84 protocols, it is based on weak coherent pulses. In this simulation, we investigate the parameter space to find limits and optimal choices of our proposed method. In addition to the non-protocol-altering clock synchronization method, we also discuss an approach that significantly improves performance in lossy channels by introducing an additional decoy state with a very high mean photon number. By eliminating the need for an extra channel capable of clock synchronization, both methods proposed potentially reduce the complexity and cost of QKD systems and improve their agility.

title: Deep Temporal Learning Models for Robust Quantum Key Integrity in Low-Latency Aviation Wireless Systems
abstract: The growing integration of quantum-resilient communication concepts into aviation and non-terrestrial networks has increased the need for secure, low-latency, and adaptive monitoring frameworks. Although quantum key distribution and post-quantum security mechanisms offer strong cryptographic foundations, their practical use in dynamic aviation environments necessitates continuous awareness of telemetry deviations, synchronization instability, and key-management risk. This paper presents a telemetry-driven temporal learning framework for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV) anomaly-risk monitoring and key-management decision support. The framework combines a long short-term memory (LSTM)-based autoencoder trained on fused multivariate UAV telemetry, calibrated feature-based anomaly-risk estimation, validation-selected operating thresholds, and a three-tier operational strategy consisting of SAFE, MONITOR, and REKEY states. The corrected chronological train-validation-test evaluation shows that the long short-term memory autoencoder (LSTM-AE) provides high-precision but conservative anomaly detection, while the calibrated HistGradientBoosting model achieves stronger ranking performance (with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve AUROC) of 0.901 and precision–recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) of 0.966. The SAFE/MONITOR/REKEY logic produces zero false positives for escalated states at the selected thresholds, although recall remains limited and several anomaly windows remain below the escalation threshold. Latency measurements indicate low computational overhead for the calibrated feature-based detector in the evaluated workstation environment, but the results do not constitute airborne edge-device or real-quantum key distribution (QKD) hardware validation. Overall, the proposed framework provides an interpretable telemetry-based risk-monitoring layer for adaptive key-management support in latency-sensitive UAV communication systems.

title: A quantitative model for embedding quantum-secure communications and evaluating communication autonomy in industrial control systems
abstract: Industrial control systems would increasingly depend on remote operation, online monitoring, and potentially autonomous control. This creates new requirements for secure, low-latency communications, and introduces new operational constraints on secret key availability, communication autonomy, and resilience under normal and abnormal conditions. We present a time-dependent quantitative model for embedding quantum-secure communications in an industrial control system and demonstrate its implementation on Purdue’s fully-digital 10-kWth research reactor (PUR-1). Using a phase-encoding decoy-state-BB84 Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) system we propose and evaluate three communication autonomy metrics: dynamic key pool size, lead time, and post-failure uptime. We establish quantitative relationships linking physical-layer QKD performance metrics, such as secret key rate (SKR) and quantum bit-error-rate (QBER), to industrial control-level communication demands defined by sampling rate, data precision, and reporting frequency. We show that for the most demanding configuration, 20 Hz sampling at 120 km, QKD coupled with AES-256 encryption required a minimum of 24 min lead time, while distances below 95 km required less than 10 min, regardless of the number of signals. These results establish experimentally verified bounds for integrating quantum cybersecurity within real-time control architectures and provide a foundation for designing quantum-resilient communication frameworks for next-generation reactors and other safety-critical industrial systems.

title: Facing the 6G: an AI-enhance quantum-secured fronthaul architecture
abstract: Amidst the development of communication technologies, the limitations of 5G communication systems, particularly in security and resource management, have become increasingly apparent. As the 6G era approaches, there are growing demands for integrated systems that ensure robust security and optimize resource utilization. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel architecture that integrates classical communication channels and quantum key distribution (QKD) channels using wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM). This innovative approach allows classical and quantum channels to coexist within a single optical fiber, improving security and fiber utilization while reducing system complexity and cost. A key contribution of this work is introducing an AI-based prediction and management module, dynamically adjusting the quantum key generation rate according to real-time usage and forecasted demand. By leveraging machine learning, the module predicts quantum key consumption patterns, ensuring that the key generation rate aligns with the system’s security and performance requirements. This approach balances key generation and usage, minimizing resource waste and enhancing the system’s overall efficiency. The feasibility of the proposed architecture is validated through an analysis of spontaneous Raman scattering (SpRS), showing the architecture maintains high key generation rates and low quantum bit error rates (QBER) under optimal system conditions. Furthermore, an analysis reveals that the AI module meets the requirement of predicting key usage and managing the key generation rate. Lastly, the feasibility is further validated by an experiment. Overall, this study presents a comprehensive framework for integrating classical and quantum channels in future 6G networks, providing enhanced security, efficiency, and scalability.

title: Mathematics and statistics in quantum computing
abstract: The integration of quantum computing into supply chain management is poised to revolutionize the field by addressing critical challenges such as data security, process optimization, and risk mitigation. At the core of this transformation lies mathematics and statistics, which form the foundation of quantum computing and cybersecurity. This chapter explores the pivotal role of mathematical disciplines—including number theory, modular arithmetic, linear algebra, and probability theory—in developing quantum algorithms for supply chain security. It highlights the application of statistical models in risk assessment, anomaly detection, and resource allocation, which are essential for safeguarding supply chain networks. The chapter delves into quantum cryptography, focusing on Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) and post-quantum cryptographic methods to ensure secure communication in supply chain ecosystems. Additionally, it examines the role of quantum-enhanced machine learning and mathematical modeling in detecting vulnerabilities, predicting risks, and optimizing operations. Case studies illustrate practical implementations of quantum technologies in supply chains, showcasing how advanced mathematics enables resilient and efficient systems. By bridging theoretical foundations and real-world applications, this chapter underscores the transformative potential of quantum computing, powered by mathematics and statistics, in advancing cybersecurity and enhancing the robustness of modern supply chains.

title: Quantam Authentication Techniques Against Emerging Threats in QKD
venue: IEEE Global Conference on Wireless Computing and Networking (GCWCN)
abstract: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is a pioneering development in secure communication, an information-theoretic secure communications protocol that is founded on quantum mechanics. However, the effectiveness of such systems which safeguard the classical communication mediums against interception and impersonation depends on the strength of the authentication mechanisms that are used in the QKD systems. The proposed study is Hybrid Quantum Authentication Framework that is based on a combination of Wegman-Carter authentication, Quantum Digital Signature (QDS), and Post-quantum Cryptography (PQC) to counter new threats of Man-in-the-Middle (MITM), replay, and key exhaustion attacks. Based on the Quantum Encryption Dataset retrieved on the Kaggle platform, the framework was experimentally tested following the dataset augmentation to incorporate the authentication parameters and simulated attack labels. The results of the experiment prove that the hybrid model proposed can attain an authentication accuracy of 98.6%, which is significantly higher than that of standalone methods, MISM and replay attack detection rates of 99 and 98, respectively. The architecture lowers the key consumption by more than 40 percent, keeps the latency at 1.28 ms and the throughput at 92 percent, proving the scalability and computational efficiency of the architecture. Comparable performance and scalability studies also indicate that the model remains highly reliable as the size of the network increases with little growth in the latency. Generally, the suggested hybrid solution is robust, flexible and effective authentication of QKD networks and a viable solution in the next-generation quantum-safe communications infrastructure that can withstand classical and quantum attackers.

title: Quantum-Powered Cryptographic Enhancements through Hybrid Approaches in Network Security
abstract: Digital communication development creates an increasing threat to data security because emerging quantum computing technologies easily overcome traditional methods of encryption. A security system that integrates traditional encrypting with quantum computing methods shows promise for enhancing safety of networks mechanisms. The Hybrid Quantum Classical–Advanced Encryption System (HQC–AES) integrates the safe symmetrical functionality of the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) with Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) procedures, specifically BB84 and E91, to ensure quantum resiliency. A secure key exchange together with real-time eavesdropper detection becomes possible through this combined approach, which maintains data confidentiality at a high level. A synthesis of post-quantum cryptography methods, such as Kyber and Falcon, safeguards traditional ways of communicating alongside quantum structures that lack comparability. The HQC–AES model provides solutions to three key cryptographic problems including secure key handling and distribution as well as encrypted transmission and long-term protection. Quantum mechanics enables protection enhancement for both conventional and quantum-based attacks by integrating it with advanced classical encryption methods. Theoretically, simulators and models show that the hybrid model maintains the technical agility of networks via several networked connections while simultaneously securing the reliability of data. The architecture delivers scalable security features to protect high-security cloud applications and financial systems and Internet of Things (IoT) resources by ensuring paramount secure communication capabilities. In safeguarding the transfer of data across several network circumstances, the suggested HQC–AES approach attained an overall accuracy of 98.7%. The fact that it is resistant to both conventional and quantum-based assaults and manages to keep data secure and intact is reflected in its excellent accuracy.

title: Quantum Inspired Security and Neuromorphic Computing for Medical Data Protections
abstract: The rapid growth of digital healthcare systems and connected medical devices has amplified the need for advanced data protection strategies. Traditional security methods face growing challenges from increasing computational power and emerging threats, including the potential impact of quantum computing. This chapter explores the integration of quantum-inspired security and neuromorphic computing as a novel approach for safeguarding sensitive medical data. Quantum-inspired techniques provide strong, future-resistant encryption by leveraging principles such as quantum key distribution and quantum-randomized algorithms, ensuring secure storage, transmission, and access control of patient information. Neuromorphic computing, modelled after the human brain, offers energy-efficient, adaptive, and parallel processing capabilities, making it ideal for edge devices like wearable sensors and Internet of Things enabled medical equipment. By combining these two technologies, healthcare systems can achieve a hybrid framework that enables quantum-resilient encryption, real-time anomaly detection, and adaptive threat monitoring, all with minimal latency and power consumption. This approach not only strengthens patient data privacy and regulatory compliance but also lays the foundation for scalable, intelligent, and secure medical data infrastructures. The chapter further discusses implementation strategies, potential applications, and future directions, highlighting the transformative potential of these emerging technologies in shaping next-generation healthcare security solutions.

title: Machine Learning for Specialized QKD Aspects: A Survey of Adaptive Protocols, Free-Space Links, 6G Integration, and Steerability-Aware Security
abstract: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) provides information-theoretic security grounded in the laws of quantum mechanics, yet practical deployment increasingly extends beyond conventional point-to-point fiber links. Several rapidly emerging QKD directions are often studied separately, including adaptive protocol and parameter support; free-space, satellite, UAV, and high-altitude platform (HAP) channels; integration with IoT and 6G networks; quantum-secured federated learning; Quantum Machine Learning (QML) assisted decision support; and steerability-aware estimation for one-sided device-independent QKD. This survey examines how Machine Learning (ML), Reinforcement Learning (RL), and QML address these specialized scenarios and organizes the literature into five thematic pillars: (I) adaptive protocol and parameter support; (II) free-space, satellite, UAV, and HAP-assisted QKD; (III) QKD for IoT, 6G, and quantum-secured federated learning; (IV) QML-assisted QKD functions; and (V) steerability-aware and one-sided device-independent QKD security estimation. For each theme, we follow a consistent problem, conventional solution, and ML/RL/QML solution structure and summarize reported gains using metrics such as accuracy, mean absolute percentage error, QBER reduction, and secret key rate improvement. We further provide thematic and cross-theme comparison tables and identify open challenges, including dataset scarcity, transferability across weather and mobility conditions, interpretability, trustworthy QML, and the boundary between ML-based decision support and security certification. This survey serves as a focused reference for adaptive, non-terrestrial, and application-integrated QKD systems.

title: Apodized fiber Bragg grating filters for efficient QKD channel separation in QKD-over-DWDM systems
abstract: This study theoretically investigates the optimal filter configuration for separating a quantum key distribution (QKD) channel from classical C-band communication channels in a discrete-variable (DV) QKD-over-dense wavelength division multiplexing (DWDM) communication system with an O-band QKD channel. Three filter configurations are analyzed and compared in terms of quantum bit error rate (QBER), secret key rate (SKR), and fiber link distance: two cascaded 1310-nm bandpass filters, a 1310-nm uniform fiber Bragg grating (FBG) with a 1310-nm circulator, and a 1310-nm apodized FBG with a 1310-nm circulator. The findings reveal that the optical filter configuration incorporating a Gaussian apodized FBG exhibits the best performance with an isolation of ~ 93 dB between 1310 nm and 1550 nm wavelengths. This optimal performance can be attributed to the Gaussian apodization profile, which effectively suppresses spectral side-lobes to enhance channel isolation while maintaining a lower insertion loss compared to the cascaded bandpass filter configuration. For 50 classical WDM channels, the QKD fiber link distance is 35.4 km with a Gaussian apodized FBG, while a configuration incorporating two cascaded 1310-nm bandpass filters yields only 18.3 km. Finally, the impact of adopting a raised-cosine apodized FBG to further increase filter channel isolation is examined. Despite a substantial increase in channel isolation by using a raised-cosine apodized FBG filter, QKD fiber link distance yields negligible improvement for this system with a QKD channel in O-band, although this filter may be highly useful for QKD channels in C- or L-bands.

title: Development of A BB84-Based Quantum Security System
venue: International Journal of Latest Technology in Engineering Management & Applied Science
abstract: The rapid advancement of quantum computing poses a serious threat to traditional cryptographic systems such as RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC), which rely on computational difficulty for security. Quantum algorithms like Shor’s and Grover’s have the potential to break or weaken these methods, putting modern communication systems at risk. To address this challenge, this work presents a quantum-safe com-munication framework that combines the BB84 Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocol with Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) techniques, aiming to ensure secure data exchange in the presence of quantum-capable adversaries. In this system, the BB84 protocol is simulated to enable secure key exchange between two parties over a virtual quantum channel. The generated key is refined through processes such as basis matching, error correction, and privacy amplification using SHA-256 to ensure reliability and secrecy. For secur-ing communication, One-Time Pad (OTP) encryption is used alongside HMAC-SHA3-256 to provide both confidentiality and message integrity. Additionally, file encryption is handled using the XChaCha20-Poly1305 algorithm, selected for its efficiency and strong protection against potential vulnerabilities like nonce reuse. To further enhance security, the framework integrates a hybrid key management approach using the Kyber-512 Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) combined with a Key Deriva-tion Function (KDF), merging classical and quantum-resistant techniques. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the system, achieving a Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) of 2.5% and successful performance in both message and file en-cryption. Overall, this work contributes toward the development of practical and resilient communication systems designed for the emerging quantum era.

title: Phase Stable Integrated Delay Line Asymmetric Mach Zehnder Interferometers Enabled by High Efficiency 3 dB Couplers for Chip Scale QKD
abstract: Precise temporal delay generation is a key requirement for asymmetric Mach-Zehnder interferometers (aMZIs) used in high-speed quantum key distribution (QKD) receivers. In this work, a compact integrated aMZI architecture based on a silicon nitride on silicon dioxide (Si3N4/SiO2) photonic platform is presented. A 3-dB directional coupler enabling accurate 50:50 power splitting at the 1550 nm telecommunication wavelength is designed and optimized. The coupling length is initially estimated from the effective index difference between the even and odd supermodes and subsequently refined using three-dimensional eigenmode expansion (EME) simulations. The optimized structure employs single-mode Si3N4 waveguides with a cross section of 1 um x 0.4 um, providing a group index close to 2 and enabling accurate delay engineering. Spectral analysis demonstrates stable 3-dB power splitting across the C-band with insertion loss below 0.5 dB and negligible power imbalance, indicating high transmission efficiency and structural symmetry. An integrated Si3N4 aMZI delay line providing a 500 ps optical delay, corresponding to a 2 GHz free spectral range (FSR), is further demonstrated. Simulations show nearly constant group delay across the 190-200 THz frequency range with sub-10 ps variation and a smooth, near-linear phase response. These characteristics enable interference visibility above 0.99, corresponding to an estimated quantum bit error rate (QBER) below 0.5 percent for gigahertz-rate time-bin QKD systems. The wideband linear phase behavior also indicates compatibility with wavelength division multiplexed (WDM) QKD architectures. The results confirm that the proposed Si3N4 integrated aMZI provides a low-loss, dispersion-controlled, and spectrally stable delay solution suitable for scalable chip-scale quantum photonic receivers.

title: Lieb-Robinson Bounds and Krylov Unforgeability: A Rigorous Framework
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: We develop a rigorous mathematical framework proving that the QKD Krylov Detector, a three-layer eavesdropper detection system for Quantum Key Distribution based on Krylov complexity and sidereal filtering, provides information-theoretically grounded security against physically realizable attacks. The central results are: (1) Krylov Locality Theorem: An eavesdropper coupling at distance d from the monitored operator cannot affect the first d Lanczos coefficients. This is an exact algebraic identity, not an approximation. (2) Perturbation Detectability Theorem: The first affected Lanczos coefficient scales as gamma^2, with computable upper and lower bound constants derived from second-order perturbation theory applied to the Lanczos recursion. (3) Information-Distortion Bound: Eve's accessible information (Holevo quantity) scales as O(gamma^2), while the Krylov distortion scales as O(gamma^4), yielding an explicit tradeoff chi <= const * sqrt(Delta_K). Verified numerically using an explicit Eve ancilla model. (4) Krylov Unforgeability Theorem: Any Hamiltonian perturbation that extracts nonzero information from the quantum channel necessarily distorts the Lanczos coefficients beyond the detection threshold. No physically realizable attack can simultaneously extract information and preserve the clean Krylov signature. (5) Coherent Attack Invariance: The Lanczos coefficients are operator-space quantities independent of any quantum state, rendering coherent and entangled attack strategies unable to circumvent detection. (6) Time-Dependent Unforgeability: Time-dependent coupling strategies gamma(t) produce strictly more distortion than constant coupling at the same average strength, by Jensen's inequality applied via a rigorous stroboscopic argument. All results include full proofs and numerical verification for chain lengths N = 6, 8, 10, 12. This work provides the formal security foundation for the QKD Krylov Detector framework developed across six prior publications. Companion code: https://github.com/quantumspiritresearch-crypto/qkd-krylov-detector

title: Next-Generation Cryptographic Security in Multi-Cloud Enterprises: AI-Enhanced Data Privacy, Protection, and Threat-Resilient Automation
venue: International Journal of Computational and Experimental Science and Engineering
abstract: Enterprise architectures with multiple clouds have brought unprecedented complexity to cryptographic security management, demanding out-of-the-box solutions that go beyond the old perimeter-based protection frameworks. The coming together of artificial intelligence and innovative cryptographic methods in protecting distributed cloud environments places high emphasis on homomorphic encryption, quantum-resistant cryptography, and self-response attack mechanisms. Cryptographic protocols integrated with machine learning models bring about dynamic key management, anomaly detection in real time, and adaptive security states reacting to changing threat profiles. Modern multi-cloud ecosystems require cryptographic frameworks that preserve data secrecy across disparate platforms with varied regulatory requirements across multiple jurisdictions. Modern advancements in AI-boosted cryptographic architecture show promise in safeguarding enterprise data across cloud borders, but there remain crucial challenges in deploying threat-resilient automation systems. Effective next-generation security deployments demand effortless collaboration among cryptographic primitives, smart automation layers, and complete governance frameworks that balance technical and organizational aspects of multi-cloud security. Zero-trust design principles remove implicit trust assumptions by using continuous verification measures, while federated learning methods facilitate collaborative security optimization without centralizing the sensitive operational information. Quantum key distribution and blockchain-based key management are new technologies that hold the promise of overcoming current constraints in multi-cloud cryptographic deployments.

title: A polarization encoder for satellite-to-ground QKD
abstract: We report the development of an optical assembly and driving electronics for a low-SWaP polarization encoder design for use in satellite-to-ground quantum communication. The optical design multiplexes multiple lasers, which are selectively excited to produce a polarization encoded output. This implementation is intrinsically stable due to the use of only polarization maintaining fiber in the combining optics. The transmitter, provides a low-cost, low-power and high-speed platform to produce polarization encoded pulses. We use the transmitter to generate 4 polarization states with 2 intensity levels via multiplexing of 8 pulsed light sources. The module can generate the polarization states H, V, D and A, which correspond to polarization angles of 0, 90, 45 and -45 degrees respectively, forming two mutually unbiased bases. The transmitter is characterized via a polarization decoder over a free-space link within a laboratory setting. We characterize the source for varying optical channel loss which is introduced between the transmitter and receiver. The transmitter employs the T12 decoy-state BB84 protocol. We explore the performance of the system with commercially available single photon detectors for two clock rates of 500 MHz and 1 GHz. We find a similar secure key rate for both repetition rates, despite the expected 3 dB gain at 1 GHz. This is a result of detector jitter hindering the performance of the QKD system, resulting in a larger QBER when detection events leak into the adjacent time bins and ultimately reduces the secure key rate.

title: Strengthening the security of end-to-end communication in photonic networks
venue: STUDIES IN ENGINEERING AND EXACT SCIENCES
abstract: The burgeoning Internet and Internet-of-Things (IoT) sectors necessitate robust cryptographic methods to ensure data security, integrity, and authentication over unsecured networks. Traditional public key cryptography, reliant on computationally hard problems, faces threats from quantum computing advancements. Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) presents a solution through the generation of unconditionally secure cryptographic keys using quantum mechanics. This paper explores the enhancement of QKD protocols to establish secure end-to-end communication in photonic networks. The proposed method involves a QKD system that generates two types of weak quantum signals: one with randomly varied intensity, polarization, or phase, and another with random frequency fluctuations. These signals are used to establish a shared key between a transmitter (Alice) and multiple receivers (Bobs) by measuring the quantum states. This dual signal approach enhances protection against Photon Number Splitting attacks and improves key length. Key Management Agents (KMAs) securely handle QKD-generated keys for data encryption before transmission, ensuring only intended recipients can decrypt the messages. The system leverages optical fiber or free-space optical links to transmit weak quantum signals and synchronization signals, facilitating key distribution even under existing network constraints. The proposed architecture allows for the secure exchange of cryptographic keys between Alice and multiple Bobs, ensuring private and authenticated communication over public channels. The approach mitigates potential eavesdropping by enabling the detection of any interception attempts through Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) estimation. This study underscores the promise of QKD as a foundational element of future communication systems, providing uncrackable quantum keys and paving the way for secure photonic networks. Incremental advancements in quantum devices, networking, and infrastructure are essential to fully realize QKD's potential for robust cryptographic security.

title: Dynamic Resource Allocation Methods in Hybrid Optical Satellite Networks for 5G/6G
venue: International Journal of Electronics and Communication Engineering
abstract: The relevance of the study is determined by the need to ensure stable Quality of Service (QoS) and efficient resource use in multi-domain telecommunication systems. Current approaches do not take into account traffic dynamics, load fluctuations, and inter-domain interaction in 5/6G architecture. The aim of the study is to develop a model for dynamic resource allocation in the Satellite Quantum Channels (SQC) → Fiber Optic Cores (FOC) → 5/6G hybrid architecture based on end-to-end cognitive orchestration, taking into account inter-segment dependencies, channel parameters, and QoS requirements. The study employed the following methods: model conceptualization, model detailing, evaluation of known methods, comparative analysis, advancing hypothesis, hypothesis justification, calculation for hybrid methods, and ranking of solutions. The results of the study demonstrated the appropriateness of implementing AI-Driven End-to-End Resource Orchestration in the SQC → FOC → 5/6G multi-segment architecture. The method demonstrated the best values: E2E latency – 0.890; throughput – 0.902; packet loss rate – 0.972; channel utilization – 0.976; blocking probability – 0.893; policy robustness – 0.813. The academic novelty is the first-proposed AI-Driven End-to-End Resource Orchestration model for cognitive resource allocation in the SQC → FOC → 5/6G hybrid network, which consistently optimizes channel parameters taking into account inter-segment dependencies, Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER), Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) throughput, Open Broadcaster Software (OBS)/ Wavelength Division Multiplexing (WDM), beamforming, and network slicing. Further research may focus on the development of cognitive cross-domain-oriented dynamic resource orchestration systems capable of providing adaptive management of spectrum, power, and time slots in hybrid communication architectures with end-to-end integration of SQC, FOC, and 5/6G domains.

title: Quantum Cryptography: Securing the Digital Future
venue: International Journal of Applied and Behavioral Sciences
abstract: In the modern digital era, where cyber-attacks, data breaches, and digital spying threaten global security, conventional cryptographic systems face increasing challenges. The rapid development of quantum computing has amplified these threats by undermining the security foundations of classical encryption algorithms such as RSA (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman) and ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography), both of which depend on the computational hardness of factorization and discrete logarithmic problems. Quantum cryptography, rooted in the principles of quantum mechanics, introduces a transformative approach that ensures theoretically unbreakable security. This paper explores the theoretical foundations, current technological developments, challenges, and future prospects of quantum cryptography. It emphasizes the transition from mathematical security to physical security, highlighting quantum key distribution (QKD), quantum random number generation, and post-quantum cryptographic frameworks. The study concludes that quantum cryptography is not merely a futuristic ideal but a necessary evolution for safeguarding the digital future in a quantum-enabled world

title: SDSE stream encryption protocol: data protection in fiber-optic networks with cryptographic strength comparable to quantum protocols
abstract: This paper presents a comparative analysis of three cryptographic approaches to securing fiber-optic data transmission: classical RSA/AES, Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) based on the E91 protocol, and Secure Dynamic Stream Encryption (SDSE). These are evaluated in terms of latency, key renewal frequency, computational load, energy efficiency, and resilience to quantum attacks. In addition to these core comparisons, we extend SDSE with a blockchain-based governance layer. This enhancement introduces auditable key management through distributed ledger technology (DLT), ensuring transparent tracking of key rotations, revocations, and policy enforcement without storing any secret material. The blockchain acts as a trust anchor for multi-node synchronization, particularly useful in federated or multi-domain environments. The combined SDSE + Blockchain framework provides a lightweight, quantum-resilient, and scalable encryption mechanism suitable for real-world deployment across conventional optical infrastructure.

title: Quantum Communication Protocol Design Based on Quantum Mechanics Principles
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel communication protocol design leveraging the principles of quantum mechanics, specifically quantum entanglement and quantum teleportation. The core claim is to enhance communication security, rate, and reliability by utilizing these quantum phenomena. The protocol is based on Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols, employing entangled particles to securely share cryptographic keys. Furthermore, it incorporates aspects of quantum teleportation to facilitate information transfer. The proposed system fundamentally departs from traditional communication protocols which are vulnerable to eavesdropping, offering a significantly higher level of security due to the inherent properties of quantum mechanics. This design addresses the limitations of classical communication methods and presents a pathway toward truly secure and high-performance communication systems. The key components of this protocol are detailed, including the entanglement generation and distribution, the key exchange process, and the information teleportation scheme. The mathematical framework underpinning these processes is presented, focusing on the core concepts of quantum information theory. ---

title: Quantum enabled cloud IOT collaboration for ultra low latency data processing in cyber physical systems
abstract: Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) are evolving in a new era of intelligent infrastructures that combine sensing and computing. However, as quantum computing and ultra-dense IoT networks tends to get expanded, traditional encrypting data and optimizing systems are insufficient to secure the data in real time. Artificial Intelligence (AI) with post-quantum cryptography and edge intelligence transforms CPS into self-adaptive ecosystems that is capable of handling threats. However, the modern systems struggle with latency management and high computational complexity that occur after quantum computing. Hence, this paper research develops an AI-Driven Quantum-Resilient Cyber-Physical System (AI-QRCPS) framework that combines three novel layers and this includes: (i) a Post-Quantum Security Layer employing lattice-based cryptography and quantum key distribution for end-to-end confidentiality, (ii) an Adaptive Intelligence Layer using Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Firefly Optimization for dynamic resource orchestration and anomaly detection, and (iii) an IoT-Edge Coordination Layer for latency-aware task scheduling using double deep Q-learning. Experimental evaluation shows that the proposed framework achieves an average latency as low as 7.9–10.7 ms, throughput up to 94.5 tasks/s, energy consumption as low as 3.3–4.8 J/task, and task completion rates exceeding 98% across varying edge/IoT node densities and bandwidths. The research designs a unified AI-driven quantum-resilient Cyber-Physical System (AI-QRCPS) framework. The results show an enhanced edge-IoT data transfer efficiency and intelligent load balancing, which gets maximized with relevance to the number of tasks processed per second under high-bandwidth conditions. The results show that the proposed framework is a flexible to build next-generation CPS networks.

title: Verified IBM Quantum Hardware Experiments: Bell State Entanglement, BB84 QKD, and Variational Quantum Circuits on ibm_fez Heron R2 and ibm_torino Heron R1
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Eight verified quantum computing jobs executed on IBM Quantum hardware (ibm_fez Heron R2, 156 qubits; ibm_torino Heron R1, 133 qubits) between January 27 and March 15, 2026. User ID: IBMid-692001DJRD. Experiments include: 1. Bell State Entanglement — 96.3% fidelity on ibm_fez Heron R2 (Concurrence C = 0.926, Tangle T = 0.858, 1,000 shots). Cross-platform benchmark: Heron R2 vs Heron R1 (+8.3 pp fidelity advantage, noise ratio 2.43×). 2. Reproducibility Test — Two independent runs of identical circuit (χ² = 2.70, p = 0.44, df = 3). H₀ not rejected: statistically indistinguishable results at 95% confidence. 3. BB84 Quantum Key Distribution — Full Alice/Eve/Bob protocol implementation. Alice baseline error 0.60% → Bob QBER 49.0% under eavesdropping (82× degradation). Experimental demonstration of the quantum no-cloning theorem. Control group design isolates eavesdropper signal from hardware noise baseline. 4. Variational Quantum Circuit (VQC) — 2-qubit circuit, 10 trained parameters with tied weights (θ₃ = θ₄), 8 CZ gates in 4 entangling layers. 4-qubit ansatz: Shannon entropy 3.885/4.000 bits (97.1%), ground-state bias confirmed (χ² = 300.94, p ≈ 0). 5. Quantum Random Number Generation (QRNG) — 8-bit outputs, 10/10 unique values per shot (range 16–254). Total: 39,010 quantum measurements across 8 jobs and 10 circuits. QPU time: 4.8 seconds. Job completion rate: 100%. All results decoded from raw IBM SamplerV2 BitArray binary archives (zlib + base64 + NumPy .npy pipeline). No simulations. Statistical validation applied throughout (Wilson 95% CIs, chi-squared tests). Stack: Qiskit Runtime SamplerV2 · QPY · OpenQASM 2.0 · Python · NumPy · SciPy Repository: https://github.com/dinohatibovicWhitepaper: https://dinohatibovic.github.io (Doc QAI-WP-2026-01-28-V4)

title: Ultra-Efficient and Scalable QoS Prediction for QKD in 7G Networks Using Fuzzy-Augmented Neural Networks
venue: IEEE Open Journal of the Communications Society
abstract: The integration of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) into prospective 7G communication systems represents a promising approach to provide information-theoretic security for future networked applications. In such environments, QKD infrastructures are expected to support heterogeneous services with diverse security and performance requirements under strict resource constraints. However, QKD performance is inherently sensitive to dynamic channel conditions, which directly affect key metrics such as the Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) and the Secret Key Rate (SKR). Since these parameters determine the achievable Quality of Service (QoS), their accurate and efficient prediction is essential for effective system optimization. In this work, we propose an ultra-efficient QoS prediction framework for QKD systems based on a Fuzzy-Augmented Neural Network (FANN) architecture. The proposed approach decomposes the prediction task into a regression stage, followed by an application-specific fuzzy inference layer that maps predictions into QoS classes. This decoupled design enables a lightweight, modular, and extensible solution suitable for resource-constrained QKD nodes. The proposed framework supports dynamic quantum channel scheduling, allowing applications to access key generation resources according to their security and throughput requirements, with direct benefits in terms of energy efficiency at both control and physical layers. Experimental results on a publicly available QKD dataset demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves comparable or improved $F_{1}$ -score performance with respect to a conventional Feed-Forward Neural Network (FFNN) classifier, while reducing inference time by over 98% and memory usage by more than 71%, even compared to FFNN models that leverage classical compression techniques, i.e., pruning and quantization.

title: Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface–Assisted Satellite-to-Ground Communication Systems
abstract: Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) have emerged as a promising technology for improving satellite-to-ground communication in future non-terrestrial networks. However, their practical deployment is constrained by hardware impairments, interference, energy limitations, regulatory power constraints, and rapidly varying link geometry, especially in low-Earth orbit (LEO) systems. These challenges become even more pronounced when RIS-assisted satellite links are extended beyond conventional radio-frequency (RF) communication to optical wireless and hybrid quantum-classical scenarios, where estimation accuracy, pointing sensitivity, and quantum bit error rate (QBER) must also be considered.This thesis develops a connected set of hardware-aware, reliability-aware, and energy-efficient design frameworks for RIS-assisted satellite communications, with extensions to optical wireless and dual-band quantum-classical links. The work begins by establishing analytical models for RIS-assisted RF satellite links under practical non-idealities, including phase quantization, element shadowing, interference, folded amplifier noise, and effective isotropic radiated power (EIRP) constraints. Based on these models, mitigation and optimization strategies are developed to preserve useful RIS gain while maintaining reliable operation under realistic propagation and hardware limitations. The framework is then extended to system-level design, where energy-efficient resource allocation and RIS selection are studied for single- and multi-surface deployments, clarifying when RIS densification improves overall performance and when its power cost outweighs its benefits.To address the significant time variation of LEO satellite channels, the thesis introduces a predictive and learning-based RIS control framework for multi-LEO environments. In this framework, channel and geometry evolution are estimated and forecasted using model-based prediction, while RIS configurations are adapted through deep reinforcement learning to improve energy efficiency and maintain robust link quality. This enables RIS control to remain responsive to satellite mobility while preserving consistency with the underlying physical channel and power models.Finally, the thesis extends the design framework beyond RF links to more advanced satellite communication settings. For optical wireless RIS-assisted links, adaptive pilot and feedback mechanisms are developed to control estimation errors under turbulence and pointing jitter. For hybrid quantum-classical operation, a dual-band RIS framework is proposed in which a shared surface supports both classical RF communication and satellite quantum key distribution by balancing signal quality and QBER objectives.The main insight of this thesis is that RIS-assisted satellite communication cannot be designed effectively through idealized beamforming models alone; instead, practical performance depends on jointly accounting for hardware imperfections, interference, energy consumption, regulatory limits, and channel dynamics within a unified framework. By connecting these aspects across RF, optical, and quantum-classical settings, this thesis provides a coherent and practically grounded methodology for the design of RIS-assisted satellite communication systems in future 6G non-terrestrial networks.

title: Integrated Evaluation of QRNG, QKD and QOTP Using NIST SP800-22 Statistical Randomness Testing
venue: International Journal of Advanced Science and Engineering
abstract: The rapid development of digital communications, cloud computing, the Internet of Things (IoT), and integrated data systems has raised concerns about securely and reliably protecting sensitive information transmitted over public and private networks.The security of cryptographic schemes such as Rivest-Shamir-Adleman (RSA) and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) relies mainly on the inherent hardness of the underlying mathematical problem.Yet the ABSTRACT: This paper evaluates a simulated quantum security pipeline integrating a Quantum Random Number Generator (QRNG), BB84 Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), and Quantum One-Time Pad (QOTP) bitwise XOR encryption.Developed using IBM Qiskit v0.45 within a controlled environment using a seed value of 12345, the proposed framework addresses the lack of multi-stage randomness testing across quantum cryptographic workflows.The execution follows a four-stage sequential workflow starting with QRNG bit generation and entropy verification, which provides the groundwork and measurement bases for BB84.Next, BB84 QKD handles qubit transmission, basis sifting, paritycheck error correction, and Toeplitz matrix hashing for privacy amplification to extract the secret key.The derived key is then used for bitwise QOTP encryption and decryption.Finally, the pipeline undergoes multi-stage statistical validation at the raw QRNG, privacy-amplified key, and ciphertext levels.Across 1,000 independent runs with 10 6 -bit systems, the framework achieved a 98.4% overall pass rate on selected NIST SP 800-22 tests at a 0.01 significance level.Under a depolarizing noise model, the Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) remained ≤ 4.2%.Using finite-key evaluation and composable security principles, the system maintained statistical integrity across all stages.The findings demonstrate a successful simulation-based proof-of-concept rather than a hardware-ready solution.Future research will focus on executing the pipeline on physical quantum hardware and evaluating performance under realistic channel loss models.

title: A Comparative Analysis of Various Identity Authentication Post Quantum Cryptography Algorithms
venue: International Conference on Electronics, Communication and Aerospace Technology (ICECA)
abstract: Single points of failure are difficult for traditional identity authentication methods to manage since they primarily depend on a reliable central entity. Furthermore, it is challenging to develop and apply these traditional systems in remote scenarios since they require storing a significant amount of public key or identity authentication data. Existing identity identification systems face serious difficulties from the introduction of quantum computing, especially with regard to the security of current cryptographic techniques. The finest authentication method for preventing unwanted access in the past was the password. As the authentication system's technology advances daily, the password gets updated to become more secure. However, the industry and researchers have been forced to discover a new option where there is no chance of theft, hacking, or password cracking due to the fragility of this traditional approach. With the introduction of quantum key distribution techniques, secure authentication has reached a new level since, unlike post-quantum cryptography, PQC can offer absolute security. Identity authentication is so crucial, and over the past three decades, a number of systems utilizing quantum resources have been put forth for identity authentication. In this research, we provide identity authentication using QKD and the falcon scheme of PQC. Intrusion detection, security level, public key size, signing time, verification time, and key generation rate with 1, 128 + Quantum, 897, 200, 100, and 100 are some of the factors that are taken into consideration when evaluating the proposed identity authentication process. The importance of switching identity authentication systems to PQC methods they are not susceptible to quantum attacks is discussed in this study. It provides a summary of identity authentication algorithms that are quantum vulnerable. By utilizing post-quantum cryptography approaches, this research adds to the continuous work towards safe, effective, and user-friendly authentication solutions. A number of PQC algorithms are examined and contrasted.

title: AI for Autonomous Operation of Small Satellite Missions
abstract: UK space industry partners Craft Prospect Ltd (CPL) and GMV deliver an advanced avionics demonstrator which incorporates cutting-edge machine learning (ML) techniques to enhance on-board autonomy for small satellite space missions. The work is funded by the European Space Agency (ESA), and the delivery partners combine expertise in embedded Artificial Intelligence (AI) and space systems engineering to target use cases for on-board autonomy which offer the best gains for a diverse range of mission types including institutional and commercial Earth observation (EO), navigation, scientific, and lunar exploration missions. _x000D_ Common technical target applications have emerged as underpinning technologies which enable the adoption of on-board autonomous operations, namely: Responsive Mission Planning and Scheduling, and Fault Detection, Isolation and Recovery (FDIR). _x000D_ Planning and scheduling are core capabilities to enable on-board autonomous operations. Tasks historically performed by ground-based operators are now replaced in large part by on-board activities which can perform short-term task planning and execution for targets of opportunity and tip and cue activities, longer-term goal based planning, and dynamic system reconfiguration. _x000D_ In every mission scenario, a large emphasis is placed on the detection and mitigation of faults by the FDIR function, in conjunction with monitoring of the spacecraft telemetry. Modern missions fuse a combination of on-board and on-ground FDIR functions to meet the needs of the mission in terms of reactiveness and computational loads. _x000D_ Two on-board processing enablers are developed to carry out autonomous mission planning and FDIR, designed to meet the requirements of a real upcoming mission scenario: ESA OPS-SAT VOLT (Versatile Optical Laboratory for Telecommunications) led by CPL. This mission requires the handling of multiple payloads and services, including activities in optical communications, quantum key distribution and hyperspectral imaging. Solutions for the VOLT mission must also meet requirements on explainability, trustworthiness and assurance of the decision-making, planning and scheduling pipeline. This demands a multi-modal approach which involves: consideration of mission-level assurance requirements on low-level AI components, a clear specification of test cases for full coverage with respect to these requirements, utilisation of relevant explainable AI (XAI) techniques and deployment of a real-time and verifiable autonomy supervisor on-board to act as a check on the AI planning solution. _x000D_ This paper describes the development of these on-board processing enablers and the cutting-edge AI technology that underpins them: reinforcement learning for responsive planning, and transformer models for anomaly detection.

title: Q-CARE-VLC: Quantum-Secured Vehicular Visible-Light Communication with Key-Continuity-Aware Handover for Smart-Ambulance Healthcare
venue: International Journal of Computer Information Systems and Industrial Management Applications
abstract: Transmission of patient telemetry, diagnostic video, electronic health records, and emergency-control information from a moving ambulance requires simultaneous low latency, high reliability, and strong confidentiality. Vehicular visible-light communication (V-VLC) offers a directional high-rate optical channel, but classical key exchange remains exposed to long-term cryptanalytic risk, and quantum key distribution (QKD) is difficult to sustain under mobility because the quantum link is sensitive to range, background light, pointing error, and handover interruption. This paper proposes Q-CARE-VLC, a dual-plane quantum-secured V-VLC architecture for connected ambulances. The architecture combines a high-rate classical vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) VLC data plane with a co-aligned decoy-state BB84 quantum key plane, trusted roadside quantum-VLC units (QVUs), a hospital key orchestrator, a dual-aperture make-before-break quantum handover mechanism, and a priority-aware quantum-key buffer. A unified analytical model is developed for vehicular optical attenuation, atmospheric loss, pointing jitter, classical achievable rate, quantum bit error rate (QBER), asymptotic decoy-state secret-key rate (SKR), key-buffer dynamics, handover interruption, and deadline-constrained medical traffic. A quantum-key-aware handover and scheduling policy gives critical physiological traffic precedence while pre-acquiring keys from the next QVU before the active quantum session is released. Monte Carlo and time-slotted simulations over a 4-km urban emergency corridor, in which all schemes share one simulator and one physical-layer parameter set, show that at an aggregate key-refresh demand of 75 kb/s, Q-CARE-VLC maintains 100% quantum-secure service continuity compared with 80.16% for a static-buffer QKD baseline and 78.77% for break-before-make QKD. At 80 km/h the modeled handover interruption fraction falls from 6.25% to 0.42%. For a daytime clear-air link, the modeled SKR is 70.62 kb/s at 40 m and 13.96 kb/s at 80 m, while the classical VLC plane remains above 83 Mb/s at 80 m. Under an 80 Mb/s aggregate medical load, the proposed scheduler satisfies the 20-ms critical-traffic deadline in 100% of slots, whereas a direct-QKD/FIFO baseline reaches only 12.69%. The results are obtained from a calibrated simulation study rather than a hardware prototype, and they establish a vehicular-healthcare architecture in which quantum key generation, mobility management, and clinical traffic prioritization are co-designed rather than treated as independent functions.

title: QUANTUM COMPUTING AND CLOUD SECURITY: FUTURE-PROOFING HEALTHCARE DATA PROTECTION
venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN COMPUTER APPLICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY
abstract: Cloud computing has emerged as the prevailing development in healthcare systems across the global market.These systems are creating and processing vast amounts of patient data that require a certain level of security.However, due to the introduction of quantum computation, the future of cryptographic techniques on which Cloud security relies is in danger.The following paper seeks to explore the compatibility of quantum computing and cloud security and regard to the protection of health data.It also includes a comprehensive analysis of the current risks, a discussion of already existing quantum-vulnerable points, and a strategy for creating a quantum-safe strategy for safe patient data storage in healthcare.The study under consideration also employs quantum cryptography and cloud structures to identify threats and create appropriate defence mechanisms.Some models explored and analyzed include Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) and hybrid cryptosystems.A simulated hospital database has brought about the fragility of some of these algorithms, a research work dubbed as quantum resilience, in order to explain how it is possible to integrate these two concepts without removing the aspects of the cloud that make it Quantum Computing and Cloud Security: Future-Proofing Healthcare Data Protection https://iaeme.com/Home/journal/IJRCAIT54 editor@iaeme.comappealing to many people, including scalability and accessibility.This indicates that there has been a major enhancement in standing against quantum attacks, specifically showing the way towards effective, sustainable and protected healthcare information systems.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Blockchain Architecture in Healthcare
abstract: Healthcare systems are increasingly data-driven through EHRs, telemedicine, and IoT-based medical devices. However, cyber threats, poor interoperability, and data tampering expose the vulnerabilities of centralized systems. Blockchain offers immutability and transparency, yet its traditional cryptography faces risks from quantum computing, which can compromise existing encryption. To address this, the chapter proposes a quantum-enhanced blockchain framework integrating post-quantum cryptography (PQC), quantum key distribution (QKD), and hybrid quantum-classical consensus. The model strengthens confidentiality, integrity, and availability (CIA) of healthcare data while ensuring interoperability and regulatory compliance. Key applications include secure EHR and genomic data management, automated patient consent handling, transparent drug supply chain monitoring, and protection of clinical research. The chapter also discusses ethical, technical, and regulatory challenges, offering insights into building resilient, quantum-secure healthcare ecosystems.

title: QUANTUM COMPUTING AND CRYPTOGRAPHY: FUTURE-PROOFING INFORMATION SECURITY PROTOCOLS
venue: Multidisciplinary Research in Computing Information Systems
abstract: Quantum computing has emerged as a disruptive technology with the potential to revolutionize various fields, including information security. Traditional cryptographic protocols, including RSA, ECC, and AES, rely on the difficulty of certain mathematical problems for their security. However, the advent of quantum computing poses a significant threat to these encryption methods, as quantum algorithms such as Shor's and Grover's algorithms can efficiently solve problems that are computationally hard for classical systems. This paper explores the implications of quantum computing on existing cryptographic systems and proposes strategies for future-proofing information security protocols. We examine the vulnerabilities introduced by quantum computing, highlight the role of post-quantum cryptography (PQC), and explore quantum key distribution (QKD) as potential solutions for ensuring the confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity of digital communications. The paper discusses various quantum-resistant algorithms and offers insights into the ongoing efforts by international standardization bodies to prepare for a post-quantum world.

title: Quantum-Secured Blockchain Ecosystems for Next-Generation Electronic Health Records
abstract: The speeding up of digitalization within the health industry and rising dependency on EHRs pose an immediate need for stronger cybersecurity architectures and protocols powered by quantum computing. The long-term confidentiality of EHRs is threatened by the assumption in cryptographic algorithms such as RSA and ECC that large-scale quantum computers will never exist, since these algorithms will be broken when they do. We propose a satisfaction-based Quantum-Secured Blockchain Ecosystem (QSBE) combining QKD with a permissioned blockchain to protect the provenance and availability of medical data while eliminating unauthorized detection from third parties. Automated and auditable patient-centric consent is enforced via smart contracts, with quantum-resistant cryptography safeguarding data against harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks. The ecosystem enables cross-institutional interoperability, regulatory oversight, and removal of single-point-of-failure. Use cases—telehealth, EHR exchange, drug traceability, emergency access—demonstrate relevance.

title: A Comprehensive Exploration of the Convergence That Will Define the Next Century of Technology
abstract: A Comprehensive Exploration of the Convergence That Will Define the Next Century of Technology Golnaz Loloei 1, Sanaz Salehian 2, Hassan Rouzrokh 3, Mohammad Rouzrokh 3, Elnaz Nazari 4 1. Department of Computer Engineering, Ke.C., Islamic Azad University, Kerman, Irangolnaz.loloei@iau.ac.ir, 0009-0000-8990-02642. Master of Science in Architecture, University of Malaya, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysiasalehian.s.sanaz@gmail.com3. Politecnico di MilanoMohammad.rouzrokh@mail.polimi.it, 0009-0001-2228-9891Hassan.rouzrokh@mail.polimi.it, 0009-0000-4473-87854. The Islamic Azad University, Science and Research Branch Tehran (Fars)nazarielnaz95@gmail.com, 0009-0001-6304-4831 Abstract The disciplines of electrical and electronic engineering are undergoing their deepest transformation since the invention of the transistor. Quantum technologies – encompassing quantum computing, quantum communication, quantum sensing, and quantum materials – are no longer confined to physics laboratories. They are becoming engineered systems that demand unprecedented precision in microwave control, cryogenic electronics, photonics, noise engineering, and high-speed signal processing. This article examines the full scope of this convergence: from the hardware foundations of superconducting and photonic quantum processors to quantum-secure networks, ultra-sensitive quantum sensors, and the emerging challenges in power and cryogenic infrastructure. Written for practising electrical engineers, engineering managers, researchers, and advanced students, it combines rigorous technical depth with forward-looking analysis of workforce transformation, industrial roadmaps, and societal impact. Keywords: Quantum Computing Hardware, Superconducting Qubits, Cryogenic Microwave Engineering, Photonic Quantum Technologies, Quantum Control Electronics IntroductionThe Third Revolution in Electrical EngineeringThe first revolution came with Maxwell’s equations and the birth of power engineering in the 1880s. The second arrived with Shockley, Bardeen, and Brattain’s transistor in 1947, followed by Kilby and Noyce’s integrated circuit, launching the digital age. Today we are living through the third: the deliberate engineering of quantum coherence at scale.Unlike previous revolutions that exploited classical physics ever more efficiently, this one requires engineers to control individual quantum systems—photons, electrons, phonons, and collective excitations—while simultaneously fighting decoherence from the surrounding thermal and electromagnetic environment. The electrical engineer is no longer merely moving charge; they are preserving phase, entanglement, and superposition across macroscopic distances and timescales. This article is structured as a complete guided tour through every major domain where advanced electrical engineering now intersects with quantum technologies. 1. Core Concepts Every Electrical Engineer Must Internalize 1.1 Quantum Bits vs Classical Bits A classical bit is a voltage above or below a threshold. A qubit can be in |0⟩, |1⟩, or any complex linear combination α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ with |α|² + |β|² = 1. The state vector lives on the Bloch sphere, and rotations are implemented by precisely tailored microwave or optical pulses. 1.2 Coherence Time (T₁, T₂) The lifetime of useful quantum information. Modern superconducting transmon qubits routinely achieve T₁, T₂ > 300 µs (IBM Condor 2024 roadmap targets 1 ms). Every nanosecond of improvement demands better materials, better shielding, and better control electronics. 1.3 Quantum Gates and Gate Fidelity A single-qubit gate is a unitary rotation; two-qubit gates (e.g. CZ, iSWAP, cross-resonance) generate entanglement. State-of-the-art two-qubit gate fidelity now exceeds 99.9 % in superconducting systems and 99.99 % in trapped-ion systems. Achieving this requires sub-picosecond timing accuracy and amplitude precision better than 0.01 %. 1.4 The DiVincenzo Criteria Applied to Engineering - Well-defined qubits - Initialisation to |00…0⟩ - Universal gate set - High-fidelity measurement - Ability to interconvert stationary and flying qubits (for networking) Every criterion maps directly onto an electrical engineering subsystem. 2. Superconducting Quantum Computing – The Microwave Engineer’s New Playground 2.1 Transmon and Fluxonium Qubits The transmon (IBM, Google, Rigetti) is a weakly anharmonic LC oscillator shunted by a Josephson junction. The fluxonium (Yale, UMass, Alice & Bob) offers longer coherence at the cost of more complex control. 2.2 Josephson Junction Fabrication Modern junctions are Al/AlOx/Al overlap or Manhattan-style junctions with critical current uniformity <1 % across 200 mm wafers (SeeQC, MIT Lincoln Lab). 2.3 Multi-Layer Microwave Design A 400+ qubit processor requires ~2,000 coaxial lines entering a dilution refrigerator. Solutions include:- 3D-integrated quantum sockets (Intel Horse Ridge + qubit chip)- Multilayer Nb-TiN airbridge crosovers- Superconducting flexible cables with <0.1 dB/m loss at 6 GHz and 20 mK 2.4 Cryogenic Low-Noise Amplification Chain Typical readout chain (2025): Qubit → Purcell filter → quantum-limited JPA or TWPA (noise temperature ~100 mK) → HEMT at 4 K (3–5 K noise temperature) → 300 K LNA → room-temperature digitizer.Latest JPAs achieve >20 dB gain with bandwidth >1 GHz and added noise <0.05 quanta. 2.5 Arbitrary Waveform Generation at Scale Modern control stacks use:- Zurich Instruments HDAWG (8 channels, 14-bit, 2.4 GS/s)- Keysight M8199B (128 GS/s interleaved)- Custom RFSoC-based boards delivering 64+ channels with <50 ps synchronisation (AWS, Google) 2.6 Crosstalk and Error Mitigation Hardware Neighbouring line coupling must be <−60 dB. Solutions: airbridge shielding, on-chip bandpass filters, spectator qubit cancellation tones. 3 Photonic Quantum Technologies – When Electrical Engineering Meets Quantum Optics 3.1 Silicon Photonics Platforms GlobalFoundries Fotonix, TowerJazz, AMF, and IMEC offer PDKs with:- Low-loss SiN waveguides (<0.1 dB/m)- High-speed Ge photodetectors- Thermo-optic and electro-optic phase shifters 3.2 Squeezed Light Generation PsiQuantum and Xanadu generate >15 dB squeezing on-chip using four-wave mixing in microring resonators pumped by 1550 nm femtosecond lasers stabilised to <1 kHz linewidth. 3.3 Single-Photon Sources - Quantum dot sources in photonic crystal cavities (delivering >70 % indistinguishability)- Spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) with PPLN waveguides 3.4 Superconducting Nanowire Single-Photon Detectors (SNSPDs) Photon-number-resolving detectors with >98 % efficiency, <15 ps jitter, and dark counts <1 Hz are now standard (PhotonSpot, Single Quantum). Cryogenic ASICs multiplex 256 detectors onto 16 output lines. 3.5 Time-Bin and Polarisation Encoding for Quantum Communication The European Quantum Internet Alliance and China’s Micius-2 roadmap rely on high-extinction-ratio (>50 dB) electro-optic modulators and ultra-low-loss fibre spools maintained at 4 K to reduce Raman scattering. 4 Trapped-Ion and Neutral-Atom Quantum Processors – Precision Analog Electronics 4.1 Surface-Electrode Paul Traps 300+ electrodes fabricated with 1 µm precision on quartz or alumina. RF voltages of 100–300 V at 20–60 MHz with <1 mV noise are required for microkelvin ion temperatures. 4.2 Global vs Individual Addressing Honeywell/Quantinuum uses global microwave horns for two-qubit gates, while IonQ and Alpine Quantum Technologies use individual 355 nm UV beams steered by 2D acousto-optic deflectors driven by 500 MS/s AWGs. 4.3 Rydberg Blockade Arrays (Cold Atoms) Pasqal and QuEra manipulate arrays of 1,000+ rubidium atoms held in optical tweezers. 300 W of 780 nm/1064 nm laser power is stabilised to sub-kHz and delivered through high-NA objectives. 5 Quantum Networking and Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) 5.1 Satellite QKD Micius (2016–present) demonstrated 1,200 km entanglement distribution. Next-generation satellites (2026–2030) will use brighter entangled sources and adaptive optics. 5.2 Terrestrial Fibre Networks Toshiba Cambridge–BT Adastral Park link (2024) achieves 500 kbit/s secure key over 120 km using twin-field QKD. Requires sub-10 fs timing synchronisation and Raman noise suppression via cryogenic fibre. 5.3 Quantum Repeaters Delft, Harvard, and AWS Center for Quantum Networking are developing entanglement swapping nodes using NV centres in diamond interfaced with 1550 nm telecom photons via electro-optic cavities. 6 Quantum Sensing and Metrology – Electrical Engineering at the Quantum Limit | Application | Quantum Advantage | Sensor Type | Electrical Engineering Role ||-------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|| Magnetometry (fT/√Hz) | NV diamond, SQUID | Ultra-low-noise current bias, lock-in detection || Inertial navigation (10⁻¹⁰ rad/s) | Cold-atom interferometers | Precision Raman laser phase control || Clocks (10⁻¹⁹ stability) | Optical lattice clocks | Frequency combs, AOM drivers, cavity stabilisation || Gravitational wave detection (10⁻²³ strain) | Optomechanical resonators | Cryogenic transducers, quantum-limited TIAs || Electric field sensing (µV/m) | Rydberg atoms | Multi-frequency RF synthesis, Stark shift readout | Real-world deployment examples:- Magnetic anomaly detection for mineral exploration (SBQuantum)- Brain imaging with optically pumped magnetometers (OPM-MEG (Cerca Magnetics, FieldLine)- GPS-denied navigation for submarines (UK DSTL cold-atom programme) 7 Power and Cryogenic Challenges – The Unsung Bottleneck A 1,000-qubit superconducting processor (2025–2027) typically consumes:- 25 kW at room temperature- 1 W at 10 mK stageScaling to logical qubits requiring 10⁶ physical qubits could exceed 100 MW without breakthroughs. Promising directions:- Dry dilution refrigerators with >3 W cooling at 100 mK (Bluefors XLDsl, Leiden Cryogenics)- Superconducting DC power lines with zero resistive loss- Cryogenic CMOS controllers operating at 4 K (Intel Horse Ridge III, 2024)- Reversible quantum computing architectures that minimise entropy generation 8 Materials and Fabrication Advances Driven by Quantum Needs | Material | Role | 2025 Status ||---------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|| Niobium titanium nitride (NbTiN) | Superconducting films | <1 µΩ·cm resistivity, Tc = 16 K || Tantalum | Qubit capacitors & inductors | Q > 50 million demonstrated (Alice&Bob Cat qubits) || 99.999 % pure aluminium | Josephson junctions | Residual resistance ratio RRR > 5,000 || Epitaxial silicon/sapphire | Travelling-wave substrates | Surface roughness <0.2 nm RMS || InP & GaAs | High-mobility 2DEGs for spin qubits | Electron mobility > 10⁶ cm²/V·s at 4 K | 9 Software and Control Stack – Where FPGA and Real-Time Systems Shine Modern quantum control hierarchy:1. Pulse-level optimisations (DRAG, Q-CTRL Boulder Opal)2. Quantum assembly (Qiskit Metal, OpenQASM 3.0)3. Compilation to analog waveforms (Superstaq, Quantum Orchestrator)4. Real-time feedback (TII Falcon board, Raytheon Quantum OS) FPGA engineers are in extremely high demand for implementing quantum error correction decoders in <1 µs latency. 10 Education, Workforce, and Economic Impact 10.1 New Degree Programmes (selected)- University of Chicago Pritzker Molecular Engineering – Quantum Science & Engineering- TU Delft QuTech Academy- University of Waterloo Institute for Quantum Computing- MIT Center for Quantum Engineering- National University Singapore CQT 10.2 Industry Demand (2025 estimates)- >30,000 quantum-skilled engineers needed globally by 2030 (McKinsey)- Median salary for cryogenic RF engineers: $180 k–$250 k USD- Shortage most acute in analog/microwave design, cryogenics, and quantum control software 10.3 Certification Pathways- IBM Qiskit Global Certification (Developer & Advocate)- Microsoft Quantum Katas + Azure Quantum credits- Xanadu Quantum Codebook ConclusionThe quantum revolution is not a replacement for classical electrical engineering—it is its most sophisticated evolution. Every classical concept—impedance matching, noise figure, phase-locked loops, feedback control—has a quantum analogue that is richer, subtler, and far more demanding.Engineers who can design a 99.999 % efficient DC–DC converters today will design 99.999 % fidelity quantum gates tomorrow. Those who master 77 K RF front-ends for 5G will soon master 20 mK microwave networks for fault-tolerant quantum computing.We are not witnessing the end of electrical engineering. We are witnessing its rebirth—at millikelvin temperatures, single-photon intensities, and attosecond timescales. The tools are new, the physics is strange, but the mission remains unchanged: to move information and energy with ever greater precision, efficiency, and control.The next golden age of electrical engineering has already begun.
